meta.title: Japan 2027
meta.about: Solo trip, Plan B (no skiing): Osaka, Koyasan, Takayama, Shirakawa-go and Hirayu Onsen. Confirmed: JQ815 BNE→SYD and the Business Classic Reward SYD→MEL→NRT on 8 Feb. Home Tue 16 Feb on QF80 + QF1256 (booked). Everything else is planned from research done 13 Sep 2026; prices marked est. need checking when booking.

days.title: Fly out via Sydney and Melbourne
days.notes: Times on this day are shown in local time at each airport. Sydney and Melbourne are one hour ahead of Queensland in February (daylight saving).

items.title: Drive Gympie → Brisbane Airport
items.notes: Book AIRPARK online beforehand (free shuttle every 10-15 min to the domestic terminal). Leaving at 6 puts you at the terminal by ~8:00. Jetstar check-in opens 2 h before and bag drop closes 40 min before departure (9:05), so 8:00-8:15 is the target.

items.title: JQ815 Brisbane → Sydney (booked, Classic Reward)
items.notes: Jetstar, economy Classic Reward. Departs 9:45 Queensland time, lands 12:20 Sydney time (Sydney is an hour ahead in February). Six hours of buffer before QF481. Bags are NOT checked through to Narita on Jetstar: you collect them in Sydney. Reward bookings include a 20 kg bag but the confirmation sometimes shows 0 kg; check it.

items.title: Collect bag, walk T2 → T3, re-check bag with Qantas for QF481
items.location: Sydney T2 baggage hall → covered walkway (7 min) → T3 Qantas bag drop
items.notes: Qantas accepts domestic bags from about 6 hours before departure, so from 12:30 you are fine. Check in for QF481 online the day before (24 h out) so you only need the bag drop. Then security and up to the lounge. If the bag drop refuses the bag early, wait landside at the T3 cafes until it opens; the lounge is airside.

items.title: Qantas Domestic Business Lounge, Sydney T3
items.location: Opposite gates 4-5, up the escalator, left door
items.notes: Your Business ticket (QF481 boarding pass) gets you in. Five hours: shower, eat lightly (the Melbourne First Lounge dinner is better), charge everything, download offline maps.

items.title: QF481 Sydney → Melbourne
items.notes: Business, A321neo, 1h35. Confirmed.

items.title: Melbourne T1 → T2 walk, then immigration
items.location: Covered walkway, one level up, 3-5 min
items.notes: Bags transfer automatically on the one booking. Allow 30-40 min for security and outbound immigration.

items.title: Qantas International First Lounge, Melbourne T2 (Titanium pass)
items.notes: Use one of your two Titanium First Lounge invitations here (show it in the Qantas app). Proper restaurant dining, so skip the Sydney lounge food and eat here. Be at the gate by ~10:45pm. Fallback if anything goes wrong with the pass: the International Business Lounge on level 1 is covered by the ticket.

items.title: QF49 Melbourne → Tokyo Narita
items.notes: Business, A330-200, 10h20, lands 7:50am Tuesday. Sleep as much as you can: Japan is only 1 hour behind Queensland, so jet lag is minimal.

days.title: Land, straight down to Osaka
days.notes: Long travel day on purpose: it puts you in Osaka the night before the calmest weekday to do Universal Studios.

items.title: Land Narita T2, immigration and customs
items.notes: Have the Visit Japan Web QR code ready (immigration + customs in one). Budget about an hour. Pick up your bag, switch on the eSIM, and withdraw ¥30,000-40,000 at the 7-Eleven ATM in the terminal (Nozawa is largely cash-only and has one foreign-card ATM, at the post office). Suica: Welcome Suica Mobile in Apple Wallet if you have an iPhone; on Android buy a physical Welcome Suica at the JR counter.

items.title: Narita Express → Tokyo Station
items.notes: ~55 min. Buy at the JR East ticket office or machine (the N’EX round-trip ticket for foreign passports, ¥5,200, is worth it because you come back this way on the 15th).

items.title: Ekiben (station bento) from Ekibenya Matsuri
items.notes: The most Japanese lunch there is. Grab one for the Shinkansen. Not a trendy place, just a shop with 200 regional bento.

items.title: Nozomi Shinkansen Tokyo → Shin-Osaka
items.notes: ~2h30, every 10 min. Reserve a seat (opens one month ahead on smart-EX). A normal suitcase under 160 cm total is fine; only bags over 160 cm need the oversized-baggage seat.

items.title: Shin-Osaka → hotel
items.location: Midosuji line south, Shin-Osaka → Namba, direct, about 13 min
items.notes: No changes, which matters when you have been awake for a day and a half. Namba is an enormous station, about 700 m end to end, and the hotel is at the JR Namba / OCAT end, so follow signs for JR Namba, not Nankai. Allow ten minutes underground on top of the thirteen on the train.

items.title: Check in at Hotel Monterey Grasmere, then shower and change
items.location: Hotel Monterey Grasmere Osaka, Namba. See Stays
items.notes: Check-in is 15:00, so you arrive about fifteen minutes early; they will take the suitcase at the desk if the room is not ready. Then actually use the hour: shower, change, repack the daypack for tomorrow. It is the single best thing you can do for a body that has been on a plane for ten hours and has to be at Universal at 7am. Ask at the desk for a high floor if it was not locked in at booking, and confirm they will handle the Yamato courier on Thursday morning. Leave for Umeda by 15:40.

items.title: Nintendo OSAKA store (optional, 45 min)
items.location: Daimaru Umeda 13F; Midosuji line Namba → Umeda is 8 min, then 5 min underground
items.notes: The official Nintendo store, exclusive merchandise, quieter than the USJ shops on Wednesday. Open 10:00-20:00, so there is slack if the trains run late. Borrowed from your friend’s Tokyo list (theirs was the Shibuya Parco store).

items.title: Grenier (Umeda): strawberry millefeuille or creme brulee
items.location: Hankyu Grand Building 1F, Kakudacho; 5 min walk from Daimaru Umeda
items.notes: French patisserie known for a very crisp, buttery millefeuille and rich custard. Takeaway counter with a few seats; 10:00-20:00. A five-minute detour on the way from Daimaru to the Nakazakicho lanes.

items.title: Walk Nakazakicho and Tenma
items.location: Nakazakicho (old wooden lanes) → Tenjinbashisuji shopping arcade → Tenma
items.notes: Low-key neighbourhoods a short train ride from Umeda. Tenjinbashisuji is 2.6 km of covered arcade where locals shop.

items.title: Tuna at Harukoma (a few pieces at the counter)
items.location: Harukoma, 5-5-2 Tenjinbashi, inside the Tenjinbashisuji arcade near 6-chome
items.notes: Osaka’s famous local sushi counter: slabs of fish cut thick, ¥100-500 a piece, mostly Osakans at the counter. Order akami, chutoro and otoro (lean, medium, fatty tuna) and stop there; gyoza is next. Expect a 20-40 min queue, it moves fast. Open 11:00-21:30. Point at the case if the menu defeats you.

items.title: Dinner in Tenma: Gyoza Club Rock Lee, then the izakaya alleys
items.location: Gyoza Club Rock Lee, 2-1-3 Ikedacho, Kita-ku (Tenma / Minamimorimachi), then under the tracks at Tenma
items.notes: Your pick. Small, loud gyoza bar a few minutes from Harukoma: crisp-bottomed gyoza, flaming mapo tofu, cheese and chilli-mayo variations; all-you-can-eat gyoza for ¥888 on weekdays with a reservation (Tuesday qualifies). Reserve on Tabelog or byFood a week or two out, or walk in early and expect a short wait. Afterwards a standing bar under the tracks for doteyaki (beef tendon simmered in miso). Home is Sakaisuji line from Minamimorimachi to Nippombashi, about 8 min, then a short walk. Early night; tomorrow starts at 7.

days.walk: 12,000-15,000 steps (stations, Umeda, the Nakazakicho and Tenma walk)

days.title: Universal Studios Japan and Super Nintendo World
days.notes: Wednesday is the calmest weekday in the window (Thursday is a public holiday, and the weekend follows). Buy the Studio Pass and an Express Pass that includes Super Nintendo World entry as soon as they go on sale for this date.

items.title: Walk to Osaka Namba, then train to Universal City
items.location: Hotel → Osaka Namba (Hanshin Namba line, ~10 min through the station) → Nishikujo → JR Yumesaki line → Universal City
items.notes: About 35 min door to gate: ten minutes walking the length of Namba station, nine on the Hanshin to Nishikujo, an easy cross-platform change, five on the JR to Universal City. Walk the station route once in daylight on the Tuesday so you are not reading signs at 7am. With the Express Pass you do not need this train: leave at 08:05 and be at the gate by 08:45.

items.title: Be at the gates before official opening
items.notes: Posted opening is usually 9:00-9:30 in February but the park regularly opens 30-60 min early. Being there by 7:45 matters if you are relying on the free timed-entry ticket. Log into the USJ app the night before and make sure the eSIM has data: the timed-entry ticket is app-only (since Jan 2026) and needs signal at the gate.

items.title: Enter USJ; claim Super Nintendo World timed entry in the app the second you are through the gate
items.notes: 1-Day Studio Pass, date-priced (¥8,900 low season up to ¥11,800 peak in 2026; Feb 2027 not published yet). If you bought an Express Pass with area entry you already have a slot and can skip the scramble.

items.title: Super Nintendo World: Mario Kart, Yoshi’s Adventure, Donkey Kong Country
items.notes: The ¥4,800 is the Power-Up Band (optional but it is the whole point of the key challenges and Bowser Jr boss fight). Ride Mario Kart first, then Donkey Kong’s Mine Cart, then wander.

items.title: Kinopio’s Cafe (Toad’s cafe)
items.notes: Reserve in the app on the day if slots show. Otherwise Yoshi’s Snack Island for a quick bite.

items.title: Rest of the park: Jurassic Park, Harry Potter area, Jaws
items.notes: Single Rider lines are the solo traveller’s cheat code and are free. February weekdays historically close around 7pm, but leave at six: Universal City to Tsuruhashi is 35-40 min and today is already a fourteen-hour day. Front-load Nintendo World in the morning and you will have done the park by then. If you want the knife, leave at four instead and see the next item.

items.title: Knife at Doguyasuji (only if you leave USJ at 16:00)
items.location: Sennichimae Doguyasuji arcade; Sennichimae line one stop to Nipponbashi then 3 min, or 13 min on foot from the hotel
items.notes: THE ONLY WINDOW ON THE TRIP. Doguyasuji is a 150 m kitchenware arcade three minutes off Dotonbori, about 50 shops, and they trade 10:00 to 18:00. Tuesday evening is Umeda, tonight you do not reach Minami until 20:45, and on Thursday you leave at nine with the suitcase already couriered. So it is this, or no knife. The cost: two hours at the tail end of USJ, which with an Express Pass is the part you will have already done. Universal City to Namba is about 30 min via Nishikujo, so a 16:00 exit puts you in the arcade by about 16:40 with well over an hour to choose. Drop it at the hotel on the way to Tsuruhashi. See Souvenirs for what to buy and why it must be checked luggage.

items.title: Yakiniku with wagyu yukke (beef tartare) in Tsuruhashi
items.location: Tsuruhashi, Korea Town: Yakiniku Tsuruhashi or one of the counters by the station
items.notes: Your beef tartare. Raw beef is only legal at licensed kitchens in Japan, so if yukke is on the menu it is the real thing: minced wagyu with egg yolk, sesame and soy. Order it first, then grilled cuts; aim to be done by about 20:30 for Dotonbori. Loop Line from Universal City, change at Nishikujo, 35-40 min. About 35 min from Universal City (Loop Line to Tsuruhashi). If USJ has flattened you, the fallback is an okonomiyaki counter near the hotel.

items.title: Dotonbori by night: the Glico sign from Ebisubashi, the canal, Hozenji Yokocho
items.location: Sennichimae line Tsuruhashi → Nippombashi (4 min), then a 5 min walk to the canal
items.notes: The neon you have seen in every photo: the Glico running man from Ebisubashi bridge, the crab and the dragon signs, the canal walkway underneath. Loud, touristy, and worth 30 minutes once. Then Hozenji Yokocho, the lantern-lit stone lane two minutes south, with the moss-covered Fudo statue people splash water on. No need to eat here; you have eaten.

items.title: Standing bars (tachinomi) in Ura-Namba
items.location: The backstreets south and east of Namba station, around Sennichimae
items.notes: Osaka’s real nightlife: no seats, order at the counter, beer ¥350 and highballs ¥300 at the cheaper ones, a small plate with each drink. More locals than tourists, and the easiest format in Japan to walk into alone. Two bars is a good evening; the person next to you will tell you where the third is. The hotel is a ten-minute walk from here, straight back through the station, which is the entire reason you are staying in Namba: no last train, no clock. Tomorrow is a 9:15 check-out for the 10:00 Koyasan train, so home by 11 anyway.

days.walk: 20,000-27,000 steps (USJ, then Dotonbori and the Namba backstreets)

culture.title: Universal Studios Japan and Super Nintendo World
culture.notes: The one early-ish start in this plan, and only if you want it: without an Express Pass the free Super Nintendo World timed-entry ticket is gone minutes after opening, so the 07:00 start matters. With an Express Pass that includes area entry (recommended, ~¥12,800) you can leave at 08:05, be at the gate by 08:45 and lose nothing. Buy the pass when the date opens (~12 Dec) and sleep in.

days.title: Osaka → Narai-juku (Edo post town) → Nozawa Onsen
days.notes: National Foundation Day, so reserve every seat a month ahead. The Shinano express runs straight through the Kiso valley, so this is the day to see rural Japan for free: hop off at Kiso-Fukushima, ride one local stop to Narai-juku, walk the 1 km Edo-period street in the snow, then carry on to Nagano. Travel hands-free: the suitcase goes ahead by courier from Osaka (see Tuesday).

items.title: Check out (daypack only), to Shin-Osaka
items.location: Namba → Shin-Osaka, Midosuji line, direct, about 13 min
items.notes: Check-out is 11:00 at the Monterey, so there is no rush at the desk. Allow about 25 min all up: eight minutes underground to the Midosuji platforms at the far end of Namba, then thirteen on the train.

items.title: Nozomi Shin-Osaka → Nagoya
items.notes: ~50 min, reserved seat.

items.title: Limited Express Shinano Nagoya → Kiso-Fukushima
items.notes: Reserved seat on the holiday. Sit on the left for the Kiso river. Buy the ticket through to Nagano with a break at Kiso-Fukushima, or two tickets; either is fine.

items.title: Local train Kiso-Fukushima → Narai
items.location: Kiso-Fukushima, Chuo line local (about every hour)
items.notes: 20 minutes. Check the local timetable when you reserve the Shinano so the connection is short.

items.title: Narai-juku: the best-preserved post town on the old Nakasendo road
items.location: Narai station → 1 km of Edo-period wooden inns and shops
items.notes: A working village, not a theme park: lacquerware workshops, a sake shop, temples up the side lanes, snow on the eaves. Narai station has no lockers but a ¥300 bag-minding desk (8:30-16:00) if you are carrying anything. Lunch here: soba or gohei-mochi (grilled rice cake with walnut-miso), the Kiso valley specialty. The Kiso Ohashi bridge and Kamidonya museum are worth 20 minutes.

items.title: Gohei-mochi and Kiso soba in Narai
items.location: Any shop on the main street with a menu outside

items.title: Local train Narai → Shiojiri, then Shinano Shiojiri → Nagano
items.notes: Local 25 min to Shiojiri, change to the Shinano (about hourly) for ~65 min to Nagano. Reserve the Shiojiri → Nagano seat too.

items.title: Hokuriku Shinkansen Nagano → Iiyama
items.notes: 12 minutes. The Nozawa Onsen Liner leaves about 10 min after each Shinkansen.

items.title: Nozawa Onsen Liner → Nozawa Onsen
items.location: Iiyama Station, bus stop out the front
items.notes: 25 min. Taxi is the fallback (¥6,000-7,000). Tell the lodging you arrive about 6pm so dinner is held.

items.title: Check in, Nozawa Onsen (5 nights)
items.location: See Stays for the shortlist and how to book
items.notes: Your suitcase should be waiting (sent by courier on Tuesday). If it is not, the daypack has tomorrow’s ski layers.

items.title: Ryokan dinner (or Wakagiri if no meals booked)
items.notes: Ryokan dinners are served at a fixed time; say so at check-in. If you are eating out, Wakagiri is the local favourite for a home-style set meal.

items.title: Oyu, the main public bathhouse
items.notes: 13 free soto-yu bathhouses run by the village. Wash first, no towel in the water, keep it quiet, no photos. Bring a small towel; expect it hot.

items.title: Send the suitcase ahead to Takayama by Yamato courier (takkyubin)
items.location: Hotel Monterey Grasmere front desk, Namba
items.notes: Do this at check-out, not earlier, or you spend two Osaka nights without your clothes. Confirm when you book that the desk takes Yamato takkyubin; full-service hotels almost always do, but this is the one morning it has to work. Hand it to the desk and ask for “takkyubin to this address”, showing the Takayama address in Japanese from the Stays page. Osaka to Gifu is next-day, so it lands at the hotel on the 12th, the day you check in. Ask for the earliest collection. Write your hotel reservation name on the delivery slip: the Takayama hotel has confirmed in writing that it will take the parcel in and hold it, and the name on the slip is how the desk matches it to you. Everything you need for Koyasan and the two nights after it goes in the daypack: two changes of clothes, toiletries, chargers, and something warm.

items.title: Check out (daypack only), walk to Nankai Namba
items.location: Hotel → Nankai Namba station, 8-10 min on foot through the arcades
items.notes: A walk rather than a train, because the hotel is in Namba. Namba is a warren, so allow the full ten minutes and follow signs for Nankai, not JR. Check-out is 11:00, so the only reason you are up is the 10:00 train.

items.title: Nankai to Gokurakubashi, cable car, bus into town
items.location: Nankai Namba → Gokurakubashi (Limited Express Koya ~80 min, or express with a change at Hashimoto ~100 min) → cable car 5 min → bus bound for Okunoin-mae, ~15 min to Okunoin-guchi (the temple stop) or Senjuinbashi (town centre)
items.notes: Buy the Koyasan World Heritage Ticket at Namba (~¥3,980): return train, cable car and unlimited Koyasan buses for two days. Reserve the limited express seat for the holiday. Drop the daypack at Shojoshin-in (Okunoin-guchi stop) before lunch if you like; the town centre is a 15-minute walk or a bus hop away.

items.title: Lunch near Senjuinbashi: soba, udon or a shojin set
Danjo Garan (the great pagoda) and Kongobuji head temple
items.notes: Kongobuji has the largest rock garden in Japan and painted sliding doors; Konpon Daito is the vermilion pagoda. Bus or 15 min walk between them.

items.title: Check in at Shojoshin-in (booked)
items.location: Okunoin-guchi bus stop, at the cemetery gate
items.notes: Show the reservation QR from the vault. Tatami room, shared baths, dinner served in your room. Curfew around 9pm. Cash payment, ¥17,600, unless the card was charged in January.

items.title: Okunoin cemetery walk to Kobo Daishi’s mausoleum
items.notes: 200,000 graves under thousand-year cedars, lanterns, snow. The single most atmospheric walk in Japan. Photography stops at the last bridge; go quiet there.

items.title: Shojin ryori dinner at the temple
items.notes: Vegetarian Buddhist cuisine, no meat or fish at all: sesame tofu (goma-dofu, the Koyasan speciality), vegetable tempura, simmered mountain vegetables, pickles, rice, soup. Served early and eaten in your room. Included in the lodging price. Honest note for a meat-eater who is lukewarm on vegetables: treat it as the experience of the night rather than the feed. The tempura, goma-dofu and rice are the easy wins; eat a proper soba or udon lunch in town, and bring a snack from Osaka for later. Tomorrow’s Hida beef in Takayama is the reward.

items.title: Okunoin night tour with a monk (optional)
items.location: Departs Eko-in, a few minutes’ walk from Shojoshin-in
items.notes: Eko-in runs an English-language night walk most evenings; ask Shojoshin-in at check-in to book you on it, and mind the 9pm curfew.

days.walk: 10,000-12,000 steps (Narai post town and the transfers)

culture.title: Osaka → Koyasan (temple lodging)
culture.notes: National Foundation Day. Koyasan is a 1,200-year-old monastery town on a forested plateau, two hours from Namba: 117 temples, a 2 km cemetery walk through giant cedars, and a night in a temple with the monks’ vegetarian dinner. Late-morning start; the suitcase went ahead to Takayama by courier this morning, so this is daypack only.
culture.walk: 12,000-15,000 steps (Okunoin is 2 km each way, plus the Garan; flat, may be icy)

days.title: Ski Nozawa, day 1
days.notes: Thursday was a stand-alone public holiday, so Friday is the comparatively quiet day before the weekend crowd arrives. Be on the Nagasaka gondola at opening (8:30) and head to Yamabiko at the top.

items.title: Ski rental fitting (pre-booked, 4 days)
items.notes: 4 days x ¥4,450 standard set (skis, boots, poles) at a village shop; the resort shop is ¥5,500/day. Book online in January with your boot size in cm: big sizes (29 cm+) run out in peak weeks. Ski wear can be rented too.

items.title: Nozawa Onsen Snow Resort, full day
items.notes: Special Pack: 1-day lift pass + ¥1,000 lunch voucher (2025-26 price; expect +5-10%). 297 ha, 1,085 m vertical, 10 km longest run (Skyline). Yamabiko for tree runs, Uenotaira for cruising.

items.title: Lunch on the mountain with the voucher
items.notes: Curry rice or ramen; the voucher covers most of it.

items.title: Onsen: try a different soto-yu (Kuma no Tearai or Shinyu)
Soba at Sobadokoro Daimon
items.notes: Hand-cut Shinshu soba. Order it zaru (cold) even in winter; it is how locals judge a soba shop.

items.title: Morning prayers and the goma fire ritual (optional)
items.notes: Worth it once in a lifetime, but nobody checks. Breakfast is served around 7:30 regardless.

items.title: Temple breakfast in your room
items.notes: Also vegetarian: rice, miso soup, tofu, pickles, a little simmered vegetable. Light by design; there are bakeries and a good lunch waiting in Takayama.

items.title: Bus, cable car and Nankai back to Namba, subway to Shin-Osaka
items.notes: Return leg is covered by the World Heritage Ticket; the subway hop is ¥300.

items.title: Nozomi Shin-Osaka → Nagoya
Kishimen noodles on the Nagoya platform
items.notes: Five-minute stand-up lunch, the Nagoya thing.

items.title: Limited Express Hida Nagoya → Takayama
items.notes: ~2h30 up the Hida river gorge; reserved seat. Hida trains run about hourly, so the exact one depends on the connection.

items.title: Check in at Temple Hotel Takayama Zenkoji (Moon room); the suitcase is waiting
items.notes: Collect the courier parcel at the desk. Tonight is the Moon room, the bigger of the two nights you have booked here, 20 m² of tatami. Do not unpack everything: tomorrow morning you check out and leave the suitcase in their store room for two nights, so set aside a daypack for Shirakawa-go and Hirayu now, while you have space to think. Tell them at check-in that you are back on Monday and leaving luggage, so the handover is expected.

items.title: Evening free
items.notes: Sanmachi old town is 10 minutes away: sake breweries with cedar balls outside (tastings for a few hundred yen), the river, Hida beef whenever you are hungry.

items.title: Hida beef dinner (whenever, wherever)
items.location: A local grill or hoba-miso restaurant off the main drag
items.notes: Hida beef on a magnolia leaf with miso is the dish. Skip the ones with touts.

days.walk: 6,000-9,000 steps (ski boots on snow; walking is short)

culture.title: Koyasan → Takayama
culture.notes: The 6:30 prayers are optional; breakfast is at a fixed time around 7:30, then a leisurely trip: down the mountain, Shinkansen to Nagoya, the Hida express up the gorge. Takayama is booked as two separate single nights now, tonight and Monday, with the suitcase living in the hotel’s store room in between. Tonight is the bigger of the two rooms. Evening free.
culture.walk: 8,000-10,000 steps (mostly trains; the old town in the evening)

days.title: Ski Nozawa, day 2
days.notes: Saturday of the long weekend: busy, so early start. Karasawa and Paradise are quieter than the gondola-top runs. Night skiing on Hikage runs on selected nights; check the board. Rental gear is easiest to fit first thing Friday, so plan on being at the shop when it opens.

items.title: Nozawa Onsen Snow Resort, full day
items.notes: Special Pack again. Explore Karasawa and Paradise; the Skyline run top to bottom late afternoon when it empties.

items.title: Mountain lunch
Onsen eggs at the Ogama
items.location: Ogama (the village’s boiling cooking spring, locals only in the water but you can watch and buy eggs nearby)

items.title: Izakaya dinner: basashi (horse sashimi) and nozawana
Check out, and leave the suitcase with the hotel
items.notes: Takayama is two separate one-night bookings, so this is a real check-out; you check back in on Monday afternoon. The hotel has confirmed in writing that it will store the suitcase for the two nights you are away. Daypack only from here: two changes of clothes, toiletries, chargers, something warm, and the crampons. Nothing you need in Shirakawa-go or Hirayu can be in the suitcase, because you will not see it again until Monday.

items.title: Miyagawa morning market (runs until noon)
items.notes: Farmers, pickles, mitarashi dango (soy-glazed rice dumplings) for a second breakfast.

items.title: Nohi bus Takayama → Shirakawa-go
items.location: Takayama Nohi Bus Center (next to the station)
items.notes: 50 min. Reserve the seat; reserved services sell out on weekends. Daypack only; the suitcase is in the hotel’s store room.

items.title: Lunch: soba or a Hida beef croquette from a stand
Shirakawa-go: Shiroyama viewpoint, Wada House, the walk between the farmhouses
items.notes: Viewpoint shuttle or a 20 min walk up. Wada House (¥400) is the big one you can go inside. Snow boots and crampons: the paths are icy.

items.title: Check in at Ootaya (the window is 15:00 to 17:00, no later)
items.notes: HARD RULES, worth respecting: check in by 17:00, phone 05769-6-1425 if you will be late, and if you arrive after 20:00 the reservation is cancelled with no refund. There is a 21:00 curfew if you go out after dinner. Six-mat tatami room, futon, dinner and breakfast included. Day-trippers leave on the last buses around five, and then the village is yours.

items.title: Blue hour: the village empty, with the lights coming on
items.notes: The reason you are staying the night. Last buses out are around five, so from then it is residents and a few dozen overnight guests. Be back for dinner at six. Skipping Shirakawa-go no Yu: it is a public bathhouse, you have tattoos, and you have a whole onsen night at Hirayu tomorrow.

items.title: Irori hearth dinner at the farmhouse
items.notes: Grilled river fish, mountain vegetables, local tofu, included in the price.

culture.title: Shirakawa-go farmhouse night (night out no. 2)
culture.notes: Check out after breakfast, leave the suitcase with the hotel and go with a daypack. Shirakawa-go’s thatched farmhouses under two metres of snow are the picture everyone has of rural Japan; it is busy from 10 to 3, and sleeping in one of the houses means you get it at dusk and dawn. Late-morning bus; no light-up event in Feb 2027.
culture.walk: 10,000-13,000 steps (village lanes and the viewpoint climb, on packed snow)

days.title: Rural day: Togakushi shrine in the snow, then Zenko-ji
days.notes: Sunday is the most crowded ski day of the trip (long-weekend Tokyo crowd), so it is the cheapest day to give up. Togakushi is a mountain shrine village above Nagano: a 2 km avenue of 400-year-old cedars leading to the inner shrine, all under deep snow in February, plus the soba the village is famous for. Back via Zenko-ji, one of Japan’s great temples. If it is dumping powder on Sunday morning, swap this for skiing and call the day a rest instead; the ski item below is kept as the alternative.

items.title: Nozawa Onsen Liner → Iiyama, Shinkansen → Nagano
items.notes: Check the Liner and Shinkansen times the night before; Sunday services are the same as weekdays.

items.title: Alpico bus 70 Nagano Station → Togakushi
items.location: Nagano Station east side, bus stop 7
items.notes: About 60 min to Chusha (middle shrine). In winter a separate winter service stops at the Okusha entrance; if the bus you are on does not, get off at Chusha and walk up the road ~30 min or take a taxi. The Zenko-ji & Togakushi 1-day bus ticket (Alpico) covers the whole day’s buses and is cheaper than singles.

items.title: Okusha cedar avenue and inner shrine
items.notes: 20 min flat walk through the cedars to the red Zuishinmon gate, then a steeper 20-30 min to the inner shrine, all on packed snow. Bring or buy simple crampons (Workman or Don Quijote sell them for ~¥1,500) and waterproof boots; ski gloves and shell are perfect. Quiet, no ropes, no gates: this is the rural Japan you asked for.

items.title: Togakushi soba at Chusha
items.location: Around Chusha (middle shrine): Uzuraya is the famous one, several quieter shops nearby
items.notes: Togakushi soba is served in small “bocchi” bundles on a bamboo tray. Order zaru, add the local wasabi. Cash.

items.title: Chusha shrine and the ninja museum village (optional)
items.notes: Chusha has an 800-year-old triple cedar at its gate. Skip the ninja stuff unless it amuses you.

items.title: Bus 70 Togakushi → Zenko-ji (Daimon stop)
items.notes: Get off at Zenkoji Daimon, not the station. Last buses back down are around 17:00-18:00; check the winter timetable.

items.title: Zenko-ji temple at dusk
items.notes: 1,400-year-old temple, the reason Nagano exists. Walk the main hall, do the pitch-black “kaidan meguri” tunnel under the altar to touch the key to paradise (¥600). The approach street (Nakamise) has oyaki and miso shops.

items.title: Nagano → Iiyama → Nozawa Onsen
items.location: Nagano Station (15 min walk or bus from Zenko-ji)

items.title: Last Nozawa dinner: oyaki, nozawana and a nabe hotpot
Pack; return rental gear tonight if the shop allows, or first thing tomorrow
ALTERNATIVE if it is a powder day: ski Nozawa instead
items.notes: Marked as skipped so it stays out of the budget. Flip the status to Planned and set the Togakushi items to Skipped if you choose to ski. Sunday lift lines ease after 2pm.

items.title: Breakfast at the hearth
items.notes: Homegrown rice and vegetables, seasonal local cooking. Set time, so be up for it.

items.title: Check out by 09:30, leave the bag, then walk the village before anyone arrives
items.notes: Check-out is 09:30, earlier than most places. They will hold your daypack afterwards, usually without fuss. The first coaches roll in around ten, so the hour before that is the second half of why you stayed: thatch, snow and nobody about. Collect the bag before the 11:10 bus.

items.title: Nohi bus Shirakawa-go → Takayama
Takayama ramen
items.location: An old shop near the station
items.notes: Thin curly noodles in a soy-shoyu broth; the town’s everyday lunch. No rush now: dinner at Hirayu is part of the room rate, so this is your proper meal of the day.

items.title: Nohi bus Takayama → Hirayu Onsen
items.location: Takayama Nohi Bus Center, next to the station
items.notes: Roughly hourly, about 1 h. No reservation needed on this route: buy at the window in the bus centre, or pay on board if it is shut. Daypack only; the suitcase is in the hotel’s store room in Takayama until Monday. Confirm the exact February times on nouhibus.co.jp in January.

items.title: Arrive, bag at the desk; room and private baths from 15:00
items.location: Hirayu no Mori, 3 min walk from the Hirayu Onsen bus terminal
items.notes: Check-in is officially 15:00 and they will hold you to it, but arriving 40 min early is normal: leave the bag at the desk and ask whether you can use the baths straight away. As a staying guest they usually say yes. Otherwise there is a tatami relaxation room and Komorebi Cafe by the front desk. The private baths are free for guests from 15:00, but they are NOT bookable: first come, first served, and there are only two. So try one the moment you are checked in, and again late at night when everyone else has gone to bed. Those are your two best windows. Do not let anyone charge you ¥3,000; that is the day-visitor price and it does not apply to you. Bath entry is normally included in the room rate; confirm that when you book so you are not paying ¥700 on top.

items.title: Settle in: tatami relaxation room, Komorebi Cafe, or the nature trail
items.notes: Mominoki is the forest restaurant on site: heated tatami room, tables facing the trees, Hida beef and cheaper set meals. Eat late so dinner can be light, or the other way round. There is also a tatami relaxation room and Komorebi Cafe by the front desk if you just want to lie down.

items.title: The forest baths as it goes dark
items.notes: Bicarbonate water, the soft kind that leaves your skin smooth. On the men’s side: seven open-air pools at different temperatures scattered through the snowy pines, two indoor baths and a sauna to warm up in. Dusk is from about half four here because the valley sits under the ridgeline. Be out by quarter to six: dinner starts at six. Reported as tattoo friendly, but confirm when you book. Even if the public baths turn out to be a problem, the free private bath is yours from 15:00 to 10:00, so the night is not wasted either way.

items.title: Dinner at restaurant Donguri: Hida beef sirloin
items.notes: Starts at 18:00 sharp, so be out of the bath by quarter to. Included in the room rate: Hida beef sirloin, well marbled, grilled at the table, with tempura, a hot pot, rice and soup. (They no longer serve the salt-grilled river fish shown in the photos.) Afterwards go back in the water: the public baths run to 21:00 and the private bath is yours until 10:00 tomorrow. No bus to catch and no closing time to beat.

items.title: If you cancel the overnight: baths and a canal town in town instead: baths and a canal town in town instead
items.notes: Associa Takayama Resort has ten outdoor baths with mountain views, 8 min by free shuttle from the station, day use with a Hida beef lunch set about ¥4,700. Takayama Green Hotel (Tenryo-no-yu) is an 8 min walk and open to day visitors 11:00-14:00 and 15:00-22:00, so it also works after dinner. Hida Furukawa, a quiet canal town with carp and two sake breweries, is 15 min by train.

items.title: Back in the water, in the dark
items.notes: The public baths run to 21:00 and the private ones are free all night. This is the hour worth staying for: snow, steam, nobody about, and no bus to catch. Try a private bath again now if you missed one earlier, because most guests have gone to bed.

culture.title: Shirakawa-go → Hirayu Onsen (night out no. 3)
culture.walk: 5,000-7,000 steps (village walk at dawn, then buses and bathing)
culture.notes: Breakfast at the hearth, a late-morning bus back, then straight onto the 12:20 bus an hour up into the Okuhida mountains. Ramen in town, an unhurried bus up, check in, the forest pools as it goes dark, dinner included, then back in the water at night with no bus to catch. The private bath is free for staying guests from 15:00 until 10:00 the next morning. Daypack only: the suitcase is in the hotel’s store room in Takayama until Monday afternoon.

days.title: Ski Nozawa, day 3 (the quiet Monday)
days.notes: The long-weekend crowd went home last night. This is the emptiest the mountain will be all trip, which is exactly why the trip now ends Tuesday.

items.title: Nozawa Onsen Snow Resort, full day
items.notes: Special Pack again. Skyline top to bottom with nobody on it; Yamabiko trees if it snowed overnight.

items.title: Mountain lunch
Onsen, then pack most of the bag
Last Nozawa dinner: basashi, nozawana, a nabe hotpot
Confirm tomorrow: Liner time, Shinkansen reservation, rental return, cash to settle the bill
Dawn bath in the snow
items.notes: First light on snow with the pools steaming is the best hour of the whole stay, and no day visitor ever sees it. The public open-air baths are open to staying guests until 08:00 and the private baths until 10:00, so you can have either; the private ones are first come, first served and nobody else will be up. Breakfast starts at 07:30 in winter, so be out by then. Worth the early alarm; it is the only one on this trip.

items.title: Breakfast at Donguri: hoba-miso
items.notes: Winter breakfast runs 07:30 to 08:30. Hoba-miso is the Hida classic: miso grilled on a dried magnolia leaf over a burner at your table, spooned onto rice. This is the local dish you would otherwise have chased in Takayama, and it comes with the room.

items.title: Nohi bus Hirayu Onsen → Takayama
items.notes: Check-out is by 10:00, so breakfast then straight to the terminal. This bus gets you back in time for the tail of the morning market and keeps the whole beef day intact. Confirm the exact time in January.

items.title: Beef day: back in Takayama, everything from here is within a 15-minute walk
items.notes: A themed free day, not a schedule. Skip anything; the only thing worth booking is dinner. One practical thing: you are not checked in yet, so you are carrying the daypack until mid-afternoon. It is small, and the market, Sanmachi and Maruaki are all a short walk from the hotel if you would rather drop it at the desk on the way past.

items.title: Miyagawa morning market: mitarashi dango and a coffee by the river
items.location: Miyagawa river bank, 10 min walk; runs until about noon
items.notes: Grilled rice dumplings brushed with soy, savoury not sweet, ¥100 a stick. Pickles, apples and crafts on the other stalls; a good wander with a coffee in hand.

items.title: Hida beef sushi at Kotte Ushi, Sanmachi
items.location: Sanmachi-suji old street, the shop with the queue
items.notes: Two pieces of seared A5 Hida beef nigiri served on a rice cracker, eaten standing in the street. The queue moves fast. A beef croquette or beef bun from the next window if you are still peckish.

items.title: Lunch at Maruaki: Hida beef from the butcher, weekday lunch set
items.location: Maruaki Hida Takayama, a few minutes from the station and the hotel; lunch 11:00-14:30 on weekdays
items.notes: A butcher with a restaurant attached. The weekday lunch sets and the yakiniku platter of A5 cut-ends are the cheapest way to eat top-grade Hida beef; go at 11:30 before the queue. Monday is a weekday, so the lunch menu runs.

items.title: Sake tasting in the old town: Funasaka (tastings 13:00-16:00) and Harada
items.location: Sanmachi-suji; look for the cedar balls hanging over the doors
items.notes: Funasaka has a tasting corner with masu cups and a courtyard; Harada is two doors along and older. A few hundred yen a pour. Buy one bottle to carry home in the suitcase.

items.title: Check in again, this time the Sakura room, and get the suitcase back
items.notes: Same building, different and smaller room (12 m²), because this is a separate booking. Collect the suitcase from their store room, put the sake bottle in it, and repack properly tonight rather than tomorrow: the Hida leaves at 9:40 and it is a travel day all the way to Narita.

items.title: Afternoon, your call: rest at the hotel, the Higashiyama temple walk, Takayama Jinya or the Hida Folk Village
items.notes: The Hida Folk Village runs a winter light-up from mid-January to the end of February, and entry after dark drops to ¥300: thatched farmhouses lit up in the snow, 10 min by bus, and it fits between about 16:30 and 18:00 before dinner. Otherwise the temple walk is a quiet 3.5 km loop above the town that starts near the hotel and earns dinner. Jinya (¥440) is the only surviving Edo provincial office; the Folk Village (¥700) is a hillside of relocated farmhouses, 10 min by bus.

items.title: Instead of coming straight back: carry on to Shinhotaka from Hirayu (40 min)
items.location: Nohi bus onward from Hirayu Onsen terminal
items.notes: You are already halfway there, so this is much easier from Hirayu than from Takayama. The most dramatic rotenburo in the region, directly under the 3,000 m Hotaka peaks, plus Japan’s only double-decker ropeway for a snow panorama of the Northern Alps. Yarimikan opens its riverside outdoor baths to day visitors; note two of its three are mixed gender. Book ahead only if boarding between Nakao and Shinhotaka Onsen. Back by dinner; the yakiniku still happens. About ¥6,000 in buses and baths.

items.title: Instead of the beef day: Gero Onsen (1 h by train from Takayama)
items.location: Hida express south, after the bus back
items.notes: One of Japan’s “three great onsen”; a bathhouse pass (Yumeguri Tegata, ¥1,500) gets you into three of the ryokan baths. Riverside foot baths are free.

items.title: Yakiniku dinner: Gyu-suke (aged A5 Hida beef, by the station), yukke if it is on the menu
items.location: Gyu-suke, a step from Takayama Station; Ajikura Tengoku is the walk-in alternative
items.notes: The beef day’s main event: several cuts you grill yourself, and a licensed raw menu (yukke with egg yolk, beef sashimi) that changes with supply, so ask. Gyu-suke takes online reservations (Tabelog or SavorJapan); book a counter seat a week or two out. Ajikura Tengoku runs a walk-in ticket system and sells out on weekends, so it is the fallback on a Monday.

culture.title: Beef day in Takayama (free-roam, all optional)
culture.notes: A themed free day: morning market, beef sushi in the old street, a butcher’s lunch, sake tasting, and aged Hida beef yakiniku at night. Everything is within a 15-minute walk of the hotel and nothing starts before 9:30. If you would rather leave town, the Okuhida or Gero onsen options replace the daytime and the yakiniku still happens.
culture.walk: 8,000-11,000 steps (bus back, then market, old street and breweries on foot)

days.title: Morning ski, then home via Tokyo
days.notes: QF80 is booked for 19:20, so the noon bus out of Nozawa is the latest sensible one.

items.title: Short morning ski (optional)
items.notes: Only if the lodging allows a late checkout and the rental shop opens early. Otherwise a slow breakfast and one last bathhouse.

items.title: Return rental gear, check out, settle in cash
Nozawa Onsen Liner → Iiyama Station
Hokuriku Shinkansen Iiyama → Tokyo
items.notes: ~1h50, reserve the seat (Hakutaka services stop at Iiyama roughly hourly).

items.title: Narita Express Tokyo → Narita T2
items.notes: Covered by the N’EX round trip ticket bought on day 1 (valid 14 days).

items.title: Narita T2: tax-free refund terminal FIRST, then check in and drop the bag
items.notes: Order matters now. Japan changed the tax-free system on 1 November 2026: you pay the full price in the shop and claim the consumption tax back at a terminal in the departure lobby, BEFORE you check your bag, with your passport. Allow 20 to 30 minutes and be able to show what you bought if asked. Do that, then check in. Arrive between 15:30 and 16:30 depending on the trains; QF80 check-in closes 18:20. Check in online 24 h before and pick a seat.

items.title: Dinner at Narita T2 food court
items.notes: Tonkatsu or ramen; last Japanese meal.

items.title: QF80 Narita → Melbourne
items.notes: Confirmed. Overnight A330, 10h25, Economy Sale fare. Try adding Economy Plus in Manage Booking. Lands Melbourne 07:45 Wed.

items.title: Free morning, pack, check out
items.notes: A last walk to the river; there are no meals at this hotel, so grab something from the konbini or the station. Nothing to catch until 9:40.

items.title: Limited Express Hida Takayama → Nagoya
items.notes: ~2h30, reserved seat.

items.title: Ichiran Nagoya Station: last ramen in Japan, in a solo booth
items.location: B1 of Hotel Resol Nagoya, a few minutes from the Shinkansen exit; open 24 h
items.notes: Ticket machine, then a one-person booth with a curtain: tonkotsu ramen, you tick the strength, richness and spice on a slip and never speak to anyone. Order the extra noodles (kaedama) with the button. 40 minutes is plenty; if the queue is long, kishimen on the platform instead.

items.title: Nozomi Nagoya → Tokyo
items.notes: ~1h40, every 10 minutes. Booked later than strictly necessary so lunch is not a sprint; Narita check-in still has two hours of slack.

items.title: Narita Express Tokyo → Narita T2
items.notes: Covered by the N’EX round-trip ticket bought on day 1.

culture.title: Takayama → Nagoya → Tokyo → home
culture.notes: No early start: the 9:40 Hida express, Shinkansen from Nagoya, Narita Express from Tokyo, at Narita by 3:30pm for the 7:20pm flight. QF80 check-in closes 18:20.

items.title: Land Melbourne T2: straight to SmartGate, collect bag, customs, Qantas domestic transfer desk, walk to T1
items.notes: 1h35 connection, protected because both flights are on the one booking; if QF80 is late Qantas rebooks you on a later Melbourne → Brisbane flight. No duty-free browsing: immigration, bag belt, customs, transfer desk, T1, gate. No time for a lounge.

items.title: QF1256 Melbourne → Brisbane
items.notes: QantasLink A220, 2h15. Confirmed.

items.title: AIRPARK shuttle to the car, lunch, drive to Gympie
items.notes: Two flights and a red-eye behind you: eat and have a proper coffee before the Bruce Highway. Home about 1:30pm.

confirmed.notes: Jetstar, Economy Classic Reward, 5,700 pts + A$43 taxes. Brisbane Terminal D (domestic). Separate booking from the Business reward, so not protected, but 6 hours of buffer. Bags not through-checked: collect at T2, re-check at T3.
Business Classic Reward. Domestic leg; check-in at Sydney T3. Same booking as QF49, so the connection is protected.

Paid fare, ¥92,570 (about A$857) for both sectors. Economy Sale fares are NOT eligible for Classic Upgrade Rewards, so a points upgrade to Business is off the table on this ticket. Economy Plus (extra legroom) is a seat product and may still be purchasable in Manage Booking with cash or points: worth trying. 30 kg checked allowance.

Same booking as QF80, so the 1h35 Melbourne connection is protected: if QF80 is late, Qantas moves you to a later Melbourne → Brisbane flight (roughly hourly) at no cost. Still, go straight to SmartGate on landing: 1h35 is enough, not generous.
Business Classic Reward. Seasonal Monday service (runs Sun/Mon/Wed/Fri, 2 Dec 2026 to late Mar 2027). Taxes paid: A$450.

legs.name: Home to Sydney, Mon 8 Feb
legs.notes: BOOKED: Jetstar JQ815 as a Classic Reward, landing 12:20 with six hours to spare. Being Jetstar it lands at T2 and the bag has to be collected and re-checked at T3, which the 6-hour buffer absorbs easily. Other options are kept below for the record.

options.label: Jetstar JQ815 Brisbane → Sydney (BOOKED)
options.notes: Economy Classic Reward. 20 kg bag should be included; confirm on the booking. Lands T2; walk 7 min to T3 and re-check the bag with Qantas.

options.label: Qantas Brisbane → Sydney, late morning
options.notes: Recommended. Park at BNE AIRPARK (A$109 for 8 days). With QF62 landing at BNE on the way home, this is the cheapest and simplest overall. 11:30 Queensland time → ~2:05pm Sydney time (AEDT): 4+ hours of buffer and lounge. Any QF flight landing before 3pm Sydney time works.

options.label: Qantas QF903 Sunshine Coast → Sydney
options.notes: 1 h from Gympie, parking ~A$90 for 8 days, no tolls. But if QF903 is cancelled the next Qantas flight lands after QF481 has gone, and the homeward flight lands at Brisbane, so you would need a A$55-85 shuttle back to the car. Times shown in Sydney time (AEDT).

options.label: Jetstar JQ787 Sunshine Coast → Sydney
options.notes: Cheapest fare, but arrives T2: collect bags, walk 7 min to T3, re-check, re-screen. No through-checking to Narita.

options.label: Qantas QF905 Sunshine Coast → Sydney, 7am (safest from MCY)
options.notes: Lowest risk if you insist on MCY: a whole day of fallback options. Long day in Sydney though (8+ hours in the lounge).

legs.name: Japan to home, Tue 16 Feb
legs.notes: BOOKED: QF80 + QF1256 as a paid Economy Sale fare. Background kept below. Big finding: the Brisbane flight (QF62) has no Premium Economy cabin at all, so “book economy and upgrade to PE” does not exist on it. The only Qantas Tokyo flight with PE is the 6:55am Haneda → Sydney. Realistic comfort upgrades: Economy Plus extra-legroom seats on the A330 (new from Sep 2026), or a Business Classic Reward if a seat appears. Points numbers marked “est.” are inferred from the Aug 2025 price rise; confirm on qantas.com when booking.

options.label: QF62 Narita → Brisbane, Economy Classic Reward
options.notes: No reward seats on 16 Feb when checked (Sep 2026). Keep an AwardFares alert running in case a batch is released; changing a booked reward costs a fee, so only switch for a Business seat. ~29,000 pts (est.) + ~A$120-170 taxes (Japan’s departure tax tripled to ¥3,000 from July 2026, so ex-Japan taxes are a little higher than older guides say). Add Economy Plus (extra legroom, ~19,500 pts or ~A$100-150 cash on similar routes) for comfort. Lands straight into Brisbane where the car is.

options.label: QF62 Narita → Brisbane, Business Classic Reward
options.notes: 82,100 pts (confirmed post-Aug-2025 price) + ~A$250-350 taxes. You have the points. Availability at Bronze in peak February is the only question; set alerts.

options.label: Jetstar JQ10 Narita → Brisbane, economy
options.notes: Cheapest points option (Jetstar table, ~24,000 pts est.; includes 20 kg bag). 787, no PE; you can bid for Jetstar Business with points + cash.

options.label: Jetstar JQ24 Osaka KIX → Brisbane (only if the trip is flipped to end in Osaka)
options.notes: Runs ~4x weekly; confirm Monday operates. Would let you do USJ on the last day and skip the Tokyo backtrack, at the cost of USJ on a Monday instead of Wednesday.

options.label: QF80 Narita → Melbourne 19:20 + QF1256 Melbourne → Brisbane 09:20 (BOOKED, cash Economy Sale)
options.notes: Booked as a paid Economy Sale fare (QF62 had no reward seats). Consequences: no points upgrade is possible on a Sale fare, so the 164k points stay in the bank for another trip; Economy Plus extra legroom may still be added in Manage Booking. 1h35 in Melbourne is protected because both flights are on one booking. Lands Brisbane 10:35 Wed, home early afternoon.

options.label: QF26 Haneda → Sydney, the only flight with Premium Economy
options.notes: 3-class A330 from Oct 2026. Economy ~36,200 pts est., PE ~74,000 pts est. Departs 6:55am (check-in from 4am, before trains run), so you would sleep at a Haneda hotel on the 15th and then still need SYD → Brisbane/Sunshine Coast. Only worth it if PE is the priority over everything else.

lounges.notes: Access comes from the Business cabin on your Classic Reward, not from status or passes. Entry opposite gates 4-5, up the escalator; Business Lounge is the left-hand door. Open until the last Qantas departure. Sydney’s First Lounge is in the international terminal (T1) and is not reachable from T3.

Airside, level 1. Covered by the Business ticket. Melbourne Airport lists a 10:15pm Monday close, but Qantas says lounges stay open until the last departure and Monday QF49 is a new service from Dec 2026: re-check the hours in January and be at the gate by 10:45pm regardless.

lounges.airport: Melbourne T2, First Lounge (level 3), Mon 8 Feb ~9pm-10:45pm
lounges.notes: Confirmed: your two passes are Qantas Money Titanium First Lounge invitations, which are valid at the Sydney, Melbourne and Los Angeles First Lounges when you are flying on a QF or JQ flight number. Use ONE here: escalator near gates 9-10 up to level 3, show the invitation in the Qantas app. Sit-down dining (the Neil Perry menu), spa if you book on arrival, showers. The second pass cannot be used on this trip (Narita has no Qantas First Lounge and you leave Sydney from the domestic terminal), so keep it for a later international departure. Third-party listings put closing at 10:15-11:15pm; be at the gate by 10:45pm. Invitations are cardholder-only and expire, so check the expiry date in the app now.

lounges.lounge: Qantas Club (via a Titanium card Qantas Club invitation)
lounges.notes: The Titanium card also gives two Qantas Club / International Business Lounge invitations a year, separate from the First Lounge ones. Qantas Club access is normally allowed when flying a Jetstar (JQ) domestic flight, so one of those invitations should open the Brisbane Qantas Club for an hour before JQ815. Check the invitation type in the app; it is a nice-to-have, not a plan.
Small terminal, four eateries, free wifi.

lounges.lounge: Economy: none. Business reward: JAL Sakura Lounge
lounges.notes: If you end up on the Business reward home, Qantas uses the JAL Sakura Lounge at Narita. In economy there is no lounge access; the 4F food court is good.
1h35 between landing and QF1256 is used up by immigration, bags, customs and the transfer. Skip the lounge.

list.name: Plan B: No skiing, Takayama base, two nights out, free days

foodGuide.title: How to tell a place is happy to have you
foodGuide.body: Green lights: a menu or prices visible outside, a ticket machine (ramen, soba, gyudon), plastic food models, a photo or English menu, a listing on Tabelog, staff who call “irasshaimase” when the door opens, and any yakiniku, okonomiyaki, udon or soba shop. Nozawa, Tenma, Fukushima, Tsuruhashi and Narai are all used to visitors; you are not intruding.

foodGuide.title: When to bow out
foodGuide.body: A sign reading 一見さんお断り (ichigen-san okotowari, “first-timers not accepted”) or 会員制 (members only); a tiny “snack” bar with a hostess and no price list; a six-seat counter where every seat is a regular and the master does not look up. Being turned away is not an insult: a small bow, “sumimasen”, and try the next door. That system is mostly Kyoto tea-house culture anyway; Osaka standing bars welcome anyone who orders a drink.

foodGuide.title: Manners that matter more than language
foodGuide.body: Order a drink first, then food. The small dish that arrives unasked (otoshi) is a cover charge, not a mistake. One drink and a couple of plates, then move on when it is crowded; angle your body to make room at a standing bar. Cash out, no tipping ever. No photos of other customers or the counter without a nod from the master. “Oishii” and “gochisosama deshita” (thanks for the meal) on the way out go a long way.

foodGuide.title: Eating alone: booths, counters and ticket machines
foodGuide.body: Solo dining is completely normal in Japan and much of the country’s best food is built for it. Easiest formats, in order: 1. Ticket-machine shops (ramen, soba, udon, gyudon at Yoshinoya or Matsuya, tonkatsu): pay the machine, hand over the ticket, sit at the counter; zero conversation. 2. Ichiran and its imitators: one-person booths with a curtain and an order slip; Dotonbori and Nagoya Station are open 24 hours. 3. Conveyor sushi (Kura, Sushiro, Hamazushi): a touch-screen at your seat, plates arrive on a belt, pay by the plate. 4. Counter seats (kauntaa) at izakaya, yakitori, okonomiyaki and yakiniku: say “hitori” (one person) with one finger up; the counter is where solo diners are put and where the cooking is. 5. Department-store basements (depachika) and konbini for a room picnic when you are done with people. Osaka’s Harukoma, Rock Lee, the Tenma alleys and Tsuruhashi yakiniku all seat singles at the counter without fuss. The only places solo is awkward are hotpot or course menus priced for two; the plan avoids them.

foodGuide.title: Carnivore, not big on vegetables: what to order
foodGuide.body: Japanese food is kind to a meat-eater. Most of the classics on this trip are meat, fish, egg, rice or noodles with vegetables as garnish rather than the point: gyoza, okonomiyaki, yakiniku, kushikatsu, doteyaki, tonkatsu, ramen, Hida beef sushi and hoba-miso beef in Takayama, char-grilled river fish at the farmhouse. Ordering tips: “niku” is meat, “sakana” is fish, “yasai” is vegetable; “yasai nashi de” (without vegetables) works at counters but is rarely needed. Set meals (teishoku) come with a small pickled or simmered vegetable side you can leave without offence; leave it untouched rather than picking it apart. The two meals where vegetables are the whole idea are both at Koyasan: the temple dinner and breakfast are strictly vegetarian, with tofu, tempura and rice as the easy wins. Plan a good lunch that day and enjoy them as the ritual they are. Shirakawa-go’s hearth dinner is river fish, mountain vegetables, tofu and rice, with the fish as the centrepiece. Tell hosts about allergies only; “I do not love vegetables” is not something to raise at a set-menu meal in Japan.

foodGuide.title: Onsen and ryokan
foodGuide.body: Shoes off at the genkan, slippers off on tatami. Ryokan dinner is at a set time; be there. In the bathhouses: wash sitting down before you get in, no towel in the water, no swimwear, quiet, no phones. Tattoos: Nozawa’s village bathhouses are relaxed but cover-up stickers are cheap insurance if you have visible ink.

staysGuide.title: Sleeping on a futon (four of your nights)
staysGuide.body: It is not the floor. A shikibuton is a thick cotton mattress on tatami, and tatami is woven rush over a springy base, so it gives. Firmer than a bed at home, nothing like boards. Back sleepers usually love it; side sleepers feel it in the shoulder and hip. The first night is the worst and most people have adjusted by the second. The fix everyone should know: ask at check-in for a second shikibuton and stack them. Almost every temple, ryokan and minshuku will do it free and without comment, because Japanese guests ask too. Say it at check-in, not at bedtime, because they lay the bedding out while you are at dinner. The other surprise is the pillow, often filled with buckwheat husks and both firm and crunchy. Ask for a soft one, or fold a towel. Your nights: Osaka is a Western bed; Koyasan (11th), Takayama (12th), Ootaya at Shirakawa-go (13th) and Takayama again (15th) are all futon; Hirayu on the 14th is a Japanese-Western room, so a bed. That is four futon nights, three of them back to back at the start, then the bed at Hirayu as a break. If the third night is telling on you, that is the one to ask for the extra shikibuton on.

staysGuide.title: Why Booking.com looks empty
staysGuide.body: Booking.com carries maybe a third of Nozawa’s beds, and Japanese inns often list only twin rooms at a 2-person price, which makes a solo search show “sold out” or silly prices. Peak weeks (this is one) also get released to Japanese sites first.

staysGuide.title: Where the rooms actually are
staysGuide.body: 1. Rakuten Travel (travel.rakuten.com, English) and Jalan: search with 1 adult; they show single-occupancy plans with meals. 2. Email the inn directly in short simple English: dates, one person, one room, ask the price with breakfast. Most reply within a day. 3. Nozawa Holidays (nozawaholidays.com) manages a dozen lodges and will answer one email with everything that still has a solo room. 4. Stay Nozawa and nozawaonsen.ski run request forms that go to several properties at once.

staysGuide.title: What to ask for
staysGuide.body: “1 person, single occupancy, 11-16 Feb, private room, breakfast included if possible.” Expect a supplement of 20-30% over the per-person twin rate. Shared bathrooms are normal and fine: you will be in the village bathhouses anyway.

staysGuide.title: If it is truly full
staysGuide.body: Togari Onsen is 20 minutes by bus across the valley and much quieter and cheaper; sleep there and bus to Nozawa for skiing. Or switch base to Akakura Onsen (Myoko), where several ryokan take single bookings on Rakuten; only the Nagano end of the plan changes. Iiyama Station has very little lodging, so do not count on it.

souvenirGuide.title: The 2.25 litre rule, which decides everything on this page
souvenirGuide.body: Australia lets one adult bring in 2.25 litres of alcohol duty free. You are travelling alone, so there is nobody to pool with. That is three ordinary 700 or 720 ml bottles and not a drop more. Go over and duty is charged on the ENTIRE amount rather than just the excess, and Australian spirits duty is among the highest in the world, so a fourth bottle can cost more in duty than it did in the shop. Buying at Narita duty free changes nothing: the limit is on what you bring in, not on where you bought it. The meter at the top of this page counts anything marked on the list or bought, so keep it honest and it will tell you when to stop.

souvenirGuide.title: A$900 of everything else
souvenirGuide.body: Separate from the alcohol, an adult gets A$900 of general goods duty free: gifts, souvenirs, electronics, leather, watches, the lot. The same trap applies, in that exceeding it means duty on all of it rather than on the excess. A knife, a Power-Up Band, a drugstore haul and some stationery will not trouble A$900. A knife plus a camera lens might. Keep a rough tally if the shopping gets ambitious, and remember things you already owned and took with you do not count.

souvenirGuide.title: Tax free changed on 1 November 2026, three months before you go
souvenirGuide.body: The old system, where the shop took the 10% consumption tax off at the till and sealed your bag, is gone. From 1 November 2026 you pay the full price in the shop and claim the tax back on the way out. At Narita, before you check your bag, go to a tax-free terminal in the international departure lobby, scan your passport, and take the refund by card, bank transfer or cash depending on the provider. You have 90 days from purchase, so everything on this trip qualifies. Two practical consequences: the refund step now comes BEFORE bag drop rather than after, and the sealed-bag nonsense where you were not allowed to open your own snacks is finished. Allow 20 to 30 minutes at Narita and be able to show what you bought if they ask.

souvenirGuide.title: Declare the food and the wood
souvenirGuide.body: Australian biosecurity is the strictest border you will cross and the incoming passenger card is not a formality. Declare all food, plant and wooden items, without exception. Commercially packaged, shelf-stable things, so sweets, sealed sauces, miso, tea, are almost always waved through once declared. Anything containing meat is prohibited outright. Fresh produce, seeds and dried plant material, including those hoba leaves, will be taken off you. The cost of declaring something that turns out to be fine is thirty seconds in the red lane. The cost of not declaring something that is not fine starts at a A$2,000 infringement notice and can reach a fine many times that.

souvenirGuide.title: Where to actually buy this stuff
souvenirGuide.body: Don Quijote is the one-stop answer for snacks, drugstore items and cheap liquor. It is chaotic, open late, tax-free, and there is one near every station you will use. Depachika, the food and drink basements of department stores like Hankyu and Daimaru in Umeda, are where the good yuzushu, the bitters and the proper sake live, and the staff will talk you through it. Doguyasuji, three minutes off Dotonbori, is the knife street. In Takayama the sake breweries sell their own bottles at the tasting, and the Miyagawa morning market has the sarubobo and the miso. Airport shopping should be the last resort rather than the plan.

souvenirGuide.title: Getting it home, given how this trip is packed
souvenirGuide.body: The suitcase leaves Osaka by courier on the morning of Wednesday the 11th and you do not see it again until Takayama on the 12th. So everything bought in Osaka, which is the USJ merch, the knife, the drugstore haul and Nintendo Osaka, has to be bought on the 9th or the 10th and packed that night. After the 11th you are carrying what you buy, which is an argument for Takayama purchases being small: a bottle, a charm, a masu cup. Bottles go in the checked bag wrapped in clothing, in the middle, never against the shell. The knife must be checked. Leave a bit of space: you will buy more than you planned to.

points.notes: Update 13 Sep 2026: the flight home was booked as a paid Economy Sale fare, which cannot be upgraded with points (Sale classes E/N/O/Q are excluded from Classic Upgrade Rewards). Only the Jetstar feeder (5,700) has used points, so about 164k stay in the bank; Economy Plus on QF80 (~19,500 pts if offered) is the one remaining use on this trip. Prices confirmed post-5 Aug 2025: NRT→BNE Business 82,100; HND/NRT→SYD/MEL Business 98,400; short domestic (Zone 1) economy 9,200 + ~A$58. Economy Tokyo→Brisbane is estimated at ~29,000 (Zone 5) and Tokyo→Sydney/Melbourne ~36,200 (Zone 6); the exact cells were not visible from here, confirm on qantas.com. Bronze members are last in the upgrade queue and are typically only considered inside 24 h of departure, so treat any upgrade as a bonus, not a plan. Qantas’ Flight Reward Finder can be searched without logging in; AwardFares has a free Qantas search with alerts.

stays.name: Anda no Mori Osaka Tennoji Tower (ex Hotel Bali Tower)
stays.type: All-inclusive urban resort hotel; the one from Instagram
stays.distance: 3 min from Tennoji station: Loop Line to USJ about 25 min (change at Nishikujo), Midosuji line 2 stops to Namba for the Koyasan train, 20 min to Shin-Osaka
stays.notes: Went viral for the guests-only LUNON lounge: patissier afternoon tea stand, 100+ free-flow drinks for up to 18 hours a day, free late-night ramen, an amenity bar with 100+ items, karaoke hour, 1,000 manga. Not literally 24 hours, and it is big, Balinese-themed and family-oriented rather than local. Worth it if you want the lounge as the evening; otherwise Dormy Inn Kitahama is quieter.

stays.name: Dormy Inn Premium Osaka Kitahama
stays.type: Business hotel with rooftop onsen bath
stays.distance: Kitahama: 20 min to Universal City by train; quiet business district by the river
stays.notes: The obvious step up, and half-wasted on you. Dormy Inn sells itself on the big communal bath, and Dormy Inn bans visible tattoos in it, so the main reason to pay the extra A$40 a night is off the table before you arrive. What is left is a nicer room, the free late-night ramen, and a calm central location at Kitahama, which is pleasant but not A$80 over two nights better than Nakatsu. Worth it only if the tattoo policy at this specific branch turns out to be relaxed, which is worth one email to ask.

stays.name: Toyoko Inn Osaka Umeda Nakatsu No.1
stays.type: Budget business hotel, 170 rooms
stays.distance: 1 min to Nakatsu (Midosuji line), 10 min walk to JR Osaka Station
stays.notes: RUNNER-UP, AND THE FALLBACK IF THE MONTEREY IS FULL OR THE PRICE JUMPS. The cheap floor, and it holds up against all three days, but the rooms are 11 to 13 m² and that is the reason the Monterey won. Shin-Osaka to Nakatsu is two Midosuji stops, about 5 minutes, so the jet-lagged arrival is as easy as it gets. Nakatsu to Namba for the Nankai on the 11th is one direct Midosuji ride, about 12 minutes, and the last trains back from Namba after the Ura-Namba bars run to around midnight. The 9 Feb evening, Nintendo Osaka at Daimaru Umeda, Grenier, Nakazakicho and Tenma, is all on the doorstep. The one weak spot is the USJ morning: you walk 10 minutes to JR Osaka Station, then it is 12 minutes and ¥200 direct to Universal City from platform 1, so leave about 06:45 for the 07:45 gates. Free breakfast (onigiri, miso soup, salad) from around 06:30, which is early enough to be useful that morning. Rooms are genuinely small, 11 to 13 m², which is tight with a big suitcase. Check-in 16:00, or 15:00 with the Club Card; check-out 10:00. The front desk handles Yamato takkyubin, which is what you need on the 11th.

stays.name: Hotel Monterey Grasmere Osaka
stays.type: 31-storey hotel, high-floor rooms with city views
stays.priceNote: Lead-in rooms from about ¥11,000; a high-floor view twin is more like ¥18,000-25,000. Budget A$180 a night and be pleased if it is less.
stays.distance: Directly connected to JR Namba; 2-3 min to Yotsubashi-line Namba, about 8 min underground to Midosuji Namba, about 10 min walk to Nankai Namba and Osaka Namba (Hanshin/Kintetsu). Dotonbori 600 m, 10 min
stays.notes: THIS IS THE ONE. BOOK IT. Ask for a high floor: the hotel guarantees floor 26 or above on its night-view rates, and it is 31 storeys, so that is about 100 m up looking over Minami. Rooms to ask for, in order: deluxe twin with city view (38 m2), corner twin (33 m2), economy double (19 m2). Even the small one is nearly double the Toyoko and the deluxe is three times it. Check-in 15:00, check-out 11:00, an hour later than the Toyoko and useful on the 11th when the courier has to be dealt with before you leave. Why it wins on THIS trip rather than in general: (1) you are in Namba, and the Wednesday night ends in the Ura-Namba standing bars, so you walk home at 23:00 instead of watching the clock for a last train; (2) Doguyasuji, the knife street, is about 13 minutes on foot or one Sennichimae-line stop to Nipponbashi and three minutes, which is the only thing that makes the kitchen knife possible at all, because those shops shut at 18:00 and every other evening is spoken for; (3) the Nankai for Koyasan is an 8 to 10 minute walk on the Thursday, with the suitcase already gone by courier; (4) Osaka Namba (Hanshin) is at the far end of the Namba complex, about 10 minutes away, and that is the USJ route via Nishikujo, about 35 minutes door to gate. ONE HONEST CAVEAT: the hotel sits at the JR Namba end of a station that is 700 m long, so most of these are a walk across Namba rather than a step out the front door. Ten minutes at 23:00 with a drink in you still beats a last train. What it costs you: roughly A$160 more than the Toyoko across the two nights, and the Tuesday evening in Umeda becomes an 8 minute Midosuji ride each way instead of a walk out the front door. Both are worth paying. Book direct or on Rakuten Travel, take the free-cancellation rate, and confirm the desk handles Yamato takkyubin for the Thursday courier.

stays.name: Swissotel Nankai Osaka
stays.type: 36-storey tower directly above Nankai Namba station
stays.priceNote: est. from USD 220; rises steeply for high floors
stays.distance: The lobby is on the 6th floor of Nankai Namba station
stays.notes: NOT CHOSEN, but the one to upgrade to if you decide the trip wants a splurge night in it. The wake-up-on-top-of-your-train option. The lobby is inside Nankai Namba station, which is the exact station the Limited Express Koya leaves from at 10:00 on the 11th, so that morning is a lift ride. Rooms run 23 to 40 m², there are 36 floors, the higher ones look out over the whole of Minami, and the top-floor restaurant does a 360-degree view. Executive floors start at 24. It is the most convenient hotel in Osaka for this particular trip and it is also roughly three times the Toyoko, which over two nights is about A$480 more. Worth it if you want the trip to have one properly nice night in it; hard to justify on logistics alone when the Monterey is a 10 minute walk away for half the price.

stays.name: Osaka Marriott Miyako Hotel, Abeno Harukas
stays.type: Floors 38 to 57 of the tallest building in Japan
stays.distance: Tennoji, 10 min from Namba on the Midosuji line
stays.notes: NOT CHOSEN. If the view were the only thing that mattered this would be the answer and nothing else is close. It occupies floors 38 to 57 of Abeno Harukas, the tallest building in Japan at 300 m, every single room is above the 38th floor, and the Deluxe City View rooms have floor-to-ceiling glass. Rooms from about 38 m². The catch is the address: Tennoji is off the axis this trip runs on. It is 10 minutes from Namba on the Midosuji line, which is fine, but it is a long way from USJ and it is not a neighbourhood you would otherwise spend an evening in. Choose it if you want to stand at a window on your first night in Japan and look at the whole city, and accept a bit more commuting for it.

stays.name: APA Hotel Osaka Umeda, or Hotel Hokke Club Osaka
stays.type: Budget business hotel, closer to the station
stays.distance: Both within a few minutes of JR Osaka Station
stays.notes: What you buy for about ¥1,000 more a night: the 10-minute walk to JR Osaka Station disappears, which is worth exactly one thing on this trip, a slightly softer alarm on USJ morning. Otherwise these are the same class of hotel as the Toyoko Inn and the rooms are, if anything, smaller at APA. Worth a look only if Nakatsu is full or the price gap closes. Hokke Club is the quieter, slightly more old-fashioned of the two and tends to have marginally bigger rooms.

stays.name: Hotel Universal Port Vita
stays.type: Official partner hotel, 10 min walk to USJ
stays.distance: Universal City: walk to the park gates, early-entry perks on some plans
stays.notes: Pay for convenience on USJ day only if the price is close. The Universal City area is a theme-park precinct, not a neighbourhood.

stays.name: Nozawa Peaks (guesthouse, book direct)
stays.type: Japanese-style guesthouse, private rooms, shared bath
stays.distance: 4 min walk to the lifts
stays.notes: Books direct for 2026-27 on its own site, English, used to solo guests. Ask for a single room rate.

stays.name: Lodge Nagano (Aussie-run lodge)
stays.type: Lodge, private room, shared bath
stays.distance: ~100 m from the slopes, short walk to the village centre
stays.notes: Affordable, easy English, solo-friendly. Also listed by Nozawa Holidays. You will be surrounded by Australians, which is the trade-off.

stays.name: Haus St. Anton (family-run pension hotel)
stays.type: 15-room boutique pension, private rooms with bath
stays.priceNote: Classic room from ~US$184; verify solo rate
stays.distance: Village, near the Nagasaka side
stays.notes: Japanese family-run, European style, non-smoking, famous jam factory downstairs. Book direct on their English page. Top of the budget but the most Banff-like small hotel in the village.

stays.name: Nozawa Onsen Hotel
stays.type: Hotel, single rooms exist
stays.distance: Village centre
stays.notes: One of the few places with proper single rooms and its own onsen. Check Rakuten Travel and Jalan for single-occupancy plans; often cheaper than Booking.com.

stays.name: Lodge Matsuya / Lodge Nakajima (local family lodges)
stays.type: Minshuku-style lodge, private room, shared bath
stays.distance: Village
stays.notes: Japanese-run, simple, warm, cheap. These are the ones that rarely show on Booking.com: use Rakuten/Jalan or email in simple English.

stays.name: Seisenso Inn (minshuku)
stays.type: Family-run minshuku, private room, shared bath
stays.distance: In the village, 5-10 min walk to Nagasaka gondola
stays.notes: Closest to the Banff-motel price point. Ask for a single tatami room with breakfast.

stays.name: Ginrei Lodge or Nozawa Springs Lodge (via Nozawa Holidays)
stays.type: Lodge, private room
stays.distance: Village
stays.notes: Nozawa Holidays manages a dozen lodges and will tell you in one email which ones still have a solo room for 11-16 Feb. Easiest single point of contact.

stays.name: Nozawa Dream Central (budget)
stays.type: 2-star, cheapest in the village
stays.distance: Central
stays.notes: Confirm it is a private room, not a dorm, before booking.

stays.name: Mid-range ryokan with dinner and breakfast (Kawamotoya, Nozawa View Hotel Shimataka)
stays.type: Ryokan, half board
stays.distance: 5-8 min to the gondola
stays.notes: Planned as the budget placeholder until something is booked. A ryokan dinner is the local-cuisine experience you asked for and solves the solo-dinner question. Search these on Rakuten Travel with 1 adult.

stays.name: Togari Onsen pension (fallback, 20 min bus from Nozawa)
stays.type: Small pensions and minshuku
stays.distance: Across the valley from Nozawa; direct bus to Nozawa 20 min, Iiyama Station 30 min
stays.notes: Quiet little ski village with its own small resort. If Nozawa is truly full, sleep here and bus over for the Nozawa ski days. Fewer restaurants; more Japanese.

stays.name: Akakura Hotel (Myoko, accepts solo bookings)
stays.type: Onsen hotel
stays.distance: Akakura Onsen village, walk to lifts
stays.notes: Explicitly takes reservations from one person. Also on Rakuten: Kounkaku (grand old ryokan), Kotobukiro, Hotel Takeda. Switching base changes only the Nagano end of the plan.

stays.name: Shojoshin-in temple lodging (booked)
stays.address: 和歌山県伊都郡高野町高野山566 (Koyasan 566, Koya-cho, Ito-gun, Wakayama)
stays.type: Temple lodging, tatami room, shared bath, dinner and breakfast
stays.priceNote: ¥17,600 incl. tax, cash at the temple
stays.distance: Central Koyasan, walk to Okunoin
stays.notes: CONFIRMED via the Shukubo Association, check-in 15:00, half board, 1 person. Shojoshin-in sits at the Okunoin cemetery gate (bus bound for Okunoin-mae, get off at Okunoin-guchi). Payment: cash at the temple, no cards (the site also lists a “scheduled advance payment date” of 12 Jan; check on the day whether the card was charged, otherwise bring ¥17,600 cash). Cancellation free until 4pm JST on 7 Feb, then 30/50/100%. Reservation number and QR in the Private vault; the QR is what you show at check-in. Night out no. 1.

stays.name: Temple Hotel Takayama Zenkoji, Moon room (night 1 of 2)
stays.address: 岐阜県高山市天満町4丁目3 〒506-0025 (Tenman-machi 4-3, Takayama, Gifu)
stays.distance: About 10-12 min walk from the station and the Nohi bus centre; near the Higashiyama temple walk
stays.type: Guesthouse inside a temple; Japanese-style [MOON] room, 20 m², futon, shared bath, kitchen and hearth
stays.notes: BOOKED and prepaid (early-bird, no meals). Free cancellation until 23:59 on 28 Jan 2027. This started as one four-night booking at A$655.58. You were only ever going to sleep in it twice, because Saturday is the Shirakawa-go farmhouse and Sunday is Hirayu, so A$327.80 of it was paying for an empty room. The hotel agreed to cancel it fee-free and let you rebook the two nights you actually use: A$326.52 in total, a saving of A$329.06. The hotel has confirmed three things in writing: they will take in the Yamato courier parcel and hold it until you arrive (write your reservation name on the delivery slip), they will store the suitcase on 13 and 14 Feb while you are at Shirakawa-go and Hirayu, and they waived the cancellation fee on the original booking. They ask to be told if you will arrive after 19:00; the plan has you there about 16:30. Address for the courier slip: 岐阜県高山市天満町4丁目3 〒506-0025 (Tenman-machi 4-3, Takayama, Gifu). The bigger of the two rooms: 20 m², three futons laid out, non-smoking. No bath or toilet in the room; the shared bath is private-use (ask at check-in whether you book a slot) and there is a full kitchen and a hearth. The rooms sit next to the temple main hall, so pack earplugs. Reservation number is in the Private vault. Alternatives if it falls through: Hotel Around Takayama, Tabino Hotel Hida Takayama, Hida Plaza Hotel.

stays.name: Temple Hotel Takayama Zenkoji, Sakura room (night 2 of 2)
stays.address: 岐阜県高山市天満町4丁目3 〒506-0025 (Tenman-machi 4-3, Takayama, Gifu)
stays.distance: About 10-12 min walk from the station and the Nohi bus centre; near the Higashiyama temple walk
stays.type: Guesthouse inside a temple; Japanese-style [SAKURA] room, 12 m², futon, shared bath, kitchen and hearth
stays.notes: BOOKED and prepaid (early-bird, no meals). Free cancellation until 23:59 on 31 Jan 2027, three days later than the first night, so diarise both.
