Same building as the Moon room but a different and smaller room (12 m², two futons, non-smoking), because this is a separate booking: you check out on Saturday morning and check in again on Monday afternoon, and the suitcase waits in their store room in between. No bath or toilet in the room; the shared bath is private-use (ask at check-in whether you book a slot) and there is a full kitchen and a hearth. The rooms sit next to the temple main hall, so pack earplugs. Last night in Japan, and there are no meals here, so repack on Monday evening rather than in the morning. Reservation number is in the Private vault.

stays.name: Hirayu no Mori, Okuhida (night out no. 3)
stays.type: Onsen lodge attached to the bathhouse; Special Japanese-Western Single Room, 16 open-air baths
stays.distance: 3 min walk from Hirayu Onsen bus terminal; 1 h by Nohi bus from Takayama
stays.notes: Plan to book: 【Half Board】premium Hida beef loin dinner + traditional Japanese breakfast, ¥14,550 in a Special Japanese-Western Single Room. A real single room at single occupancy, so no solo supplement, which was the main risk. Meals are at restaurant Donguri: dinner 18:00 (Hida beef sirloin), winter breakfast 07:30-08:30 (hoba-miso). Private baths are free for guests from 15:00 but first come, first served with no reservations, and there are only two. Men’s baths: 2 indoor, 7 open-air, sauna. No air conditioning in the rooms, and Hirayu can sit below freezing around the clock in February. Prepaid by credit card through Time Design, so CONFIRM THE TATTOO POLICY BEFORE PAYING and read the cancellation terms; prepaid agency bookings are often strict. Cheaper plans exist from ¥11,000 (room only or B&B) if you would rather eat elsewhere. The reason to stay: the private bath is ¥3,000 for day visitors but FREE for guests, and their window runs 15:00 to 10:00 the next morning, so you can use it after dark and before breakfast. The public forest baths are open to guests until 08:00 too. Reported as tattoo friendly; confirm in writing, though the free private bath covers you either way. Hotel Hirayunomori Annex is the cheaper sister property 3 min away. Their own site is Japanese-only, so use Booking.com.

stays.name: Ootaya, gassho-zukuri guesthouse (night out no. 2)
stays.address: 岐阜県大野郡白川村荻町1807 〒501-5627 (1807 Ogimachi, Shirakawa-mura, Ono-gun, Gifu). Tel 05769-6-1425
stays.type: Thatched gassho farmhouse in Ogimachi; 6-mat tatami, non-smoking, dinner and breakfast
stays.distance: In the village
stays.notes: BOOKED and prepaid by card. Package: Traditional Gassho style house, 1 night with 2 meals. Reservation number is in the Private vault. Check in 15:30; the window closes at 17:00 and you must phone 05769-6-1425 if you will be late. Arrive after 20:00 and the booking is cancelled with no refund. Curfew 21:00. Check out by 09:30, and they will hold your bag afterwards. Cancellation: 20 percent from 15 days out (29 Jan), 50 percent from 7 days, 70 percent the day before, 100 percent inside 24 hours. Dates and guest numbers CANNOT be amended online: changing either means cancelling and rebooking from scratch. Note their standing warning that all their cooking uses dashi (fish stock) and sake.

food.where: Every meal; buy a bag from a village grandma’s shop to take home
food.why: The village’s signature food. Every family pickles its own; you will be offered it constantly.

food.where: Street stalls near Oyu and at Nagano Station
food.why: Grilled-then-steamed buns filled with nozawana, pumpkin or bean paste. The Nagano snack.

food.where: Main street, 100+ years in the Katagiri family
food.why: Hand-cut buckwheat noodles, cold zaru style with dipping sauce. Old shop, no fuss.

food.where: Any village izakaya
food.why: Nagano speciality, served with ginger and soy. Try it once.

food.where: Ogama, top of the village
food.why: Eggs slow-cooked in the 90°C spring. Locals cook their vegetables there too; it is the village kitchen.

food.where: Main street
food.why: Home-style teishoku that locals actually eat. Not a ski-bar.

food.where: Any counter with a hotplate in Fukushima or Tenma (avoid the Dotonbori queues)
food.why: Osaka’s home cooking. Sit at the teppan, order “buta-tama”, watch it made.

food.dish: Gyoza at Gyoza Club Rock Lee (Tenma)
food.where: 2-1-3 Ikedacho, Kita-ku; 5 min from Tenma or Minamimorimachi stations
food.why: The gyoza bar you asked for. Crisp-bottomed gyoza, flaming mapo tofu, cheese and chilli-mayo gyoza, ¥888 all-you-can-eat on weekdays with a reservation. Planned for the Tuesday 9 Feb dinner. Book on Tabelog or byFood, or walk in early.

food.where: Izakaya alleys under the tracks at Tenma station
food.why: Beef tendon simmered in miso, and the deep-fried skewers Osaka is known for, in the part of town where office workers drink. No double dipping.

food.where: A stand with a queue of locals, not the ones with English menus
food.why: Octopus balls, Osaka’s thing. Eat them standing up, straight away.

food.where: Usami-tei Matsubaya (the shop that claims to have invented it, near Minami-Semba)
food.why: Udon in dashi with sweet fried tofu, Osaka’s soul food. Old shop, cheap.

food.dish: Yakiniku and wagyu yukke (beef tartare) in Tsuruhashi (Korea Town)
food.where: Tsuruhashi station area; Yakiniku Tsuruhashi lists wagyu yukke
food.why: Osaka’s Korean neighbourhood; smoky yakiniku joints, nothing trendy about it. Yukke is the Japanese-Korean beef tartare and only licensed places may serve it, so a menu that has it is safe. Planned for the Wednesday night after USJ.

food.where: Shinsekai, a few doors from the famous Daruma
food.why: If you do go to Shinsekai, this is the locals’ pick over the tourist-famous Daruma. About ¥2,000 a head.

food.where: Tenjinbashisuji arcade, 5-chome
food.why: The tuna stop. Thick-cut akami, chutoro and otoro at a loud local counter for a few hundred yen a piece. On the Tuesday walk, before gyoza.

food.dish: Endo Sushi at the Central Fish Market (early option)
food.where: Osaka Central Wholesale Market, Noda; 5:00-14:00, closed Sundays and holidays
food.why: Since 1907, five pieces of whatever landed that morning, tuna included, eaten standing by the market. Only fits at 6:00 on the USJ morning (Noda is two stops from Universal City), which is earlier than you like, so it is an option, not the plan. Check the market’s calendar; some Wednesdays are market holidays.

food.dish: Ichiran (solo ramen booths): Dotonbori 24 h, Umeda Hankyu Higashi-dori
food.where: Dotonbori main and south buildings, 4 min from Namba exit 14 (24 hours); Umeda branch in the Hankyu Higashi-dori arcade near the hotel
food.why: The famous one-person booths. Not planned into a slot in Osaka because every meal there is already spoken for, but it is the answer at midnight, in the rain, or when you cannot face another menu. Ticket machine, curtain, slip of paper, done.

food.dish: Ichiran Nagoya Station: the last ramen
food.where: B1 Hotel Resol Nagoya, a few minutes from the Shinkansen exit; 24 hours
food.why: Planned for the Tuesday 16 Feb lunch between the Hida and the Nozomi home. Solo booth, no talking, 40 minutes door to door.

food.where: Backstreets south and east of Namba station, around Sennichimae
food.why: Tachinomi: no seats, cheap drinks, a small plate with each, and conversation that happens on its own. Planned for the Wednesday night after yakiniku and the Dotonbori neon. Optional extra: the 20 min Tombori canal cruise (¥2,000, last boat 21:00) only if you leave USJ early.

food.where: Umeda branch, Hankyu Grand Building 1F (also Kitahama)
food.why: Strawberry millefeuille with a loud crunch and a rich custard; the pastry stop on the Tuesday afternoon between the Nintendo store and Nakazakicho.

food.dish: Wagyu burger at Kitan Hibiki (optional swap)
food.where: Hozenji Yokocho, 3 min from Namba station exit 14
food.why: Charcoal-grilled 100% wagyu burger, ranked in the World’s 101 Best Burgers. Only served 12:00-15:00 and 17:00-19:00, and it needs a reservation. The only slot is Wednesday evening straight from USJ, leaving the park by about 17:30, in place of the okonomiyaki dinner. Yakiniku the rest of the evening.

food.where: Fukumaru-dori, one Loop Line stop from Osaka Station
food.why: A workers’ dining street lined with small izakaya and bars; a good alternative base for dinner if the hotel is around Fukushima.

food.where: Ekibenya Matsuri, Tokyo Station
food.why: Regional lunch boxes to eat on the Shinkansen. Pick one from Nagano or Niigata.

food.where: Nagano Station area
food.why: Nagano is miso country. Warm you up after the Shinano train.

food.where: Super Nintendo World
food.why: The one touristy meal that is worth it: themed, and you are already inside.

food.where: Your temple, dinner and breakfast
food.why: Buddhist vegetarian cooking at its source. The sesame tofu is Koyasan’s own; buy a block from Hamadaya to take on the train.

food.where: A small grill off Sanmachi
food.why: Local beef cooked on a magnolia leaf over miso. The regional dish, not a tourist invention.

food.where: An old shop in the centre
food.why: Soy broth, thin curly noodles, what locals eat for lunch.

food.dish: Mitarashi dango at the morning market
food.where: Miyagawa market stalls
food.why: Soy-glazed, savoury not sweet here. Breakfast while you browse.

food.dish: Hida beef sushi at Kotte Ushi
food.where: Sanmachi-suji old street
food.why: Two pieces of seared A5 beef nigiri on a rice cracker, eaten in the street. The Takayama snack. Planned for the Monday beef day.

food.where: Maruaki Hida Takayama, a few minutes from the station; weekday lunch 11:00-14:30
food.why: A butcher with a restaurant: lunch sets and a platter of A5 cut-ends at a fraction of dinner prices. Monday beef-day lunch.

food.dish: Aged Hida beef yakiniku at Gyu-suke
food.where: By Takayama Station; reserve on Tabelog or SavorJapan
food.why: Female A5 Hida beef, dry-aged, grilled at your counter; ask for yukke or beef sashimi from the licensed raw menu. The beef day’s dinner. Ajikura Tengoku is the walk-in fallback.

food.where: Funasaka and Harada breweries on Sanmachi-suji; Funasaka tastings 10:00-12:00 and 13:00-16:00
food.why: Cedar balls over the door mean a brewery. A few hundred yen a pour in a masu cup; one bottle for the suitcase.

food.where: Your farmhouse
food.why: Char-grilled river fish, mountain vegetables, tofu, cooked over the sunken hearth. This is why you stay the night.

food.where: Watanabe or Kaba breweries, Hida Furukawa (15 min by train)
food.why: Two old breweries in a canal town nobody visits; ¥300 tastings, no queue.

food.where: A small sushi-ya near the station (ask the hotel)
food.why: Takayama is far from the sea, so the good places fly fish in daily and the locals know which ones; a counter seat is the solo traveller’s best dinner.

souvenirs.name: Yuzu liqueur (yuzushu)
souvenirs.where: Depachika liquor floors at Hankyu or Daimaru in Umeda, any Don Quijote, or a neighbourhood liquor shop
souvenirs.why: The best spritz base Japan makes and the one you cannot buy properly at home. Sharp and floral rather than sweet like limoncello, so it holds up over prosecco and soda instead of drowning in it. Look for Kimino, Tosa Buntan, or whatever regional one the shop pushes.
souvenirs.notes: Around ¥1,500 to ¥3,000. Check the label for the alcohol strength: some yuzushu is 8% and closer to a wine, some is 20% and a proper liqueur. You want the stronger one for spritzes.

souvenirs.name: Sake: one bottle from Funasaka or Harada
souvenirs.where: Sanmachi-suji, Takayama, at the Mon 15 Feb tasting
souvenirs.why: Already in the plan and the one bottle with a story attached, since you will have stood in the brewery and tried it. A junmai or a sparkling sake travels better than a daiginjo, which wants refrigeration and does not forgive a warm cargo hold.
souvenirs.notes: Ask them to wrap it. Sake does not keep forever once open, so this is a bottle to drink rather than to shelf.

souvenirs.name: The Japanese Bitters: yuzu, shiso, umami
souvenirs.where: Department store liquor floors, bar-supply shops, or the better Don Quijote branches
souvenirs.why: The smartest thing on this page. Three 30 ml bottles barely touch the 2.25 L allowance, they are near-impossible to buy in Australia, and a couple of dashes turns an ordinary spritz into something nobody else at the table is drinking. Yuzu for brightness, shiso for the herbal edge, umami if you want to be strange about it.
souvenirs.notes: About ¥2,000 a bottle. If the allowance gets tight, these are the last thing you should drop, because they are the highest flavour per millilitre you can carry.

souvenirs.name: Ki No Bi Kyoto Dry Gin
souvenirs.where: Department store liquor floors, good bottle shops, or Narita duty free on the way out
souvenirs.why: The one Japanese gin genuinely worth the allowance: yuzu, hinoki, bamboo and sansho pepper, distilled in Kyoto. It lands in Australia at A$110 to A$130 when you can find it at all. Makes a gin spritz that tastes like nowhere else.
souvenirs.notes: With the umeshu dropped, this now fits: the yuzushu, the sake and the bitters come to 1.51 L, so adding this lands you at 2.21 L of the 2.25 you are allowed. That is the whole allowance gone, and nothing else with a cork can come home. Worth knowing: Roku and Nikka Coffey Gin are both on Australian shelves already, so do not spend the allowance on those.

souvenirs.name: Shiso or sakura liqueur
souvenirs.why: The novelty pick that turns out to be good. Shiso is minty and grassy and makes a startlingly fresh spritz; sakura is floral and works better in spring than in February. Neither exists in Australia in any real way.

souvenirs.name: A masu cup from the tasting
souvenirs.why: The little cedar box you drink sake out of. Costs a few hundred yen, weighs nothing, smells like the brewery for years, and is the cheapest good souvenir on this list.

souvenirs.name: Power-Up Band
souvenirs.where: The cart in front of Super Star Plaza, or the 1-UP Factory shop inside Super Nintendo World
souvenirs.why: Half a ticket and half a souvenir. You need one to do the Key Challenges and collect the digital coins in the area, so it earns its keep on the day, and afterwards it works as an amiibo on a Switch at home. Six to choose from: Mario, Luigi, Peach, Daisy, Toad and Yoshi.
souvenirs.notes: About ¥4,900, up from ¥3,800 a couple of years ago. Buy it first thing rather than on the way out, because the whole point is using it in the area. The Universal Studios Store will engrave it.

souvenirs.name: 1-UP Factory: the park-exclusive Mario things
souvenirs.why: This is the shop whose stock you cannot get anywhere else, including at Nintendo Osaka. Question blocks, 1-UP mushroom tins, Bowser and Toad things, the area-branded apparel. If you want a Nintendo souvenir that says USJ rather than just Nintendo, it is here.
souvenirs.notes: Wed 10 Feb. Use a ride locker rather than carrying bags onto Mario Kart, and remember the shops near the entrance stay open after the rides stop.

souvenirs.name: Nintendo Osaka is a different shop
souvenirs.where: Daimaru Umeda, 13th floor. Already on the plan for Tue 9 Feb at 16:00
souvenirs.why: Worth knowing the two do not overlap much. Nintendo Osaka carries the general Nintendo range, plush, apparel, Zelda and Splatoon and Animal Crossing. USJ carries the Super Nintendo World park merchandise. If you want both, you need both stops, and they fall on consecutive days anyway.

souvenirs.name: A Japanese kitchen knife
souvenirs.where: Doguyasuji, the covered kitchenware arcade a few minutes from Dotonbori
souvenirs.why: The single best thing most people bring back from Japan. Doguyasuji is three minutes off Dotonbori, which is where the Wednesday night ends. A Sakai-forged gyuto or santoku runs ¥8,000 to ¥25,000, they will sharpen it and often engrave your name in kanji while you wait, and it will outlive you.
souvenirs.notes: TIMING IS THE PROBLEM, not the money. Doguyasuji shops shut at 18:00, and the plan only reaches Minami at 20:45 on the Wednesday. The slot is now in the itinerary as an optional item: leave USJ at 16:00 instead of 18:00 on Wed 10 Feb and you are in the arcade by 16:35 with 85 minutes, with the hotel on the way back to drop it. That is the only window, because Tuesday evening is Umeda and Thursday you leave at nine with the suitcase already gone. MUST go in the checked bag. A knife in hand luggage gets confiscated at Kansai or Narita and nobody will post it on for you. Buy it in Osaka before the 11th so it rides in the suitcase with the courier. If you have never used a carbon-steel knife, buy stainless: carbon rusts if you leave it wet and most people do.

souvenirs.name: Sarubobo charm
souvenirs.where: Anywhere in Takayama, and every stall at the Miyagawa morning market
souvenirs.why: The faceless red doll is Takayama's own. A few hundred yen, weighs nothing, and is the one souvenir that actually says where you were rather than just "Japan".

souvenirs.name: Ichii ittobori yew carving
souvenirs.why: Takayama's traditional woodcarving, unpainted yew that darkens with age. Small pieces are affordable and it is the local craft rather than a souvenir-shop import.
souvenirs.notes: Tick the wooden-items box on the Australian incoming card. Finished, treated timber is almost always fine; declaring it costs you nothing and not declaring it is the expensive mistake.

souvenirs.name: Regional KitKats and konbini sweets
souvenirs.where: Don Quijote, konbini, station gift shops, airport before the gate
souvenirs.why: The easy crowd-pleaser and the flavours really are regional: matcha, sake, wasabi, hojicha, whatever is seasonal in February. Cheap enough to hand out.
souvenirs.notes: Declare them. Commercially packaged, shelf-stable confectionery is almost always allowed straight through; it is the not-declaring that causes trouble.

souvenirs.name: Hoba miso (the miso, not the leaves)
souvenirs.where: Takayama, Miyagawa market and the shops on Sanmachi
souvenirs.why: The magnolia-leaf miso you will have eaten for breakfast at Hirayu. The paste itself is a processed food and travels fine.
souvenirs.notes: Buy the miso, skip the dried leaves. Dried plant material is exactly what biosecurity takes off you, and the leaves are the part you can improvise at home with baking paper.

souvenirs.name: Yuzu kosho, furikake, a good soy
souvenirs.where: Depachika food halls, or a supermarket for a fifth of the price
souvenirs.why: The three things that actually get used at home rather than sitting in a cupboard. Yuzu kosho in particular is expensive and mediocre in Australia and cheap and excellent there.
souvenirs.notes: Nothing containing meat, ever: no jerky, no meat-filled snacks, no instant ramen with a meat sachet. That is a prohibited import, not a declare-and-see.

souvenirs.name: Drugstore haul
souvenirs.where: Matsumoto Kiyoshi or Don Quijote, anywhere, open late
souvenirs.why: The genuinely better-and-cheaper category. Biore UV sunscreen is the best on earth and a third of the Australian price, Hada Labo lotion, Salonpas patches, Eve painkillers, sheet masks by the dozen.
souvenirs.notes: Cheap enough that this is where the tax-free threshold gets crossed without noticing. Keep the receipts together.

souvenirs.name: Stationery from Loft or Tokyu Hands
souvenirs.where: Umeda, on the Tuesday afternoon walk
souvenirs.why: Uni Kuru Toga mechanical pencils, Pilot pens, Midori and Kokuyo notebooks. Small, light, cheap, and the quality gap over what you can buy at home is real.

souvenirs.name: Work out who actually gets something
souvenirs.where: Decide before you go, buy at Don Quijote on the last night
souvenirs.why: The trap is leaving this to the airport and paying three times for worse things. A list of names written down now turns into one 20-minute shop later. KitKats, a sarubobo each and a sheet mask covers most people.

budget.label: Brisbane Airport AIRPARK, 9 days
budget.notes: A$99/week + A$10/day. Book online; sometimes cheaper than drive-up. MCY would be ~A$90 but needs a A$55-85 shuttle back from Brisbane on the way home.

budget.label: Travel insurance with snow-sports cover, 10 days
budget.notes: Must include skiing. Medicare does not cover Japan.

budget.label: Travel insurance, 10 days (no snow sports needed)
eSIM, 10 days data
budget.notes: Ubigi or Airalo; install before you leave.

budget.label: Onsen towels, ski socks, souvenirs, contingency
Suica top-ups (local trains, buses, vending machines)
USJ Express Pass 4 with Super Nintendo World entry (optional but recommended)
budget.notes: Nintendo-inclusive Express Pass 4 variants (e.g. “Mine Cart & Jaws”) were ~¥12,800 in 2026; Express Pass 7 ¥17,800-21,800. Names change every season: buy any Express Pass whose description includes “Super Nintendo World Area Entry” (ideally with Mario Kart and Mine-Cart Madness). Sells out on popular dates.

checklist.text: Check what your two lounge passes actually are: Qantas app → Complimentary Lounge Invitations → type (Titanium / Platinum One / General / Domestic) and expiry
checklist.notes: Only Titanium or Platinum One invitations open the Melbourne First Lounge. General/Domestic ones add nothing on this trip because the Business ticket already covers the Business lounges.

checklist.text: Keep a free AwardFares alert on QF62 NRT→BNE and QF80 NRT→MEL for 16 Feb 2027 (Business especially)
checklist.notes: Seats are released in batches. The paid Sale fare cannot be upgraded, but a Business Classic Reward could replace it if one appears and the Sale fare’s cancellation terms make it worthwhile (Sale fares are usually non-refundable, so probably not).

checklist.text: Book Nozawa Onsen accommodation for 11-16 Feb, 5 nights (long weekend; the village sells out)
checklist.notes: Email the minshuku directly for a single room, or Booking.com. Ask about single-occupancy pricing and whether dinner is included.

checklist.text: Book Hotel Monterey Grasmere Osaka, 9-11 Feb, high floor with a city view
checklist.notes: DECIDED: the Monterey Grasmere in Namba. Two nights: check in Tue 9 Feb, check out Thu 11 Feb. Ask for the deluxe twin with city view (38 m2) or the corner twin (33 m2), and say you want a high floor: their night-view rates guarantee floor 26 or above out of 31. Budget about A$180 a night; the lead-in rooms are cheaper if the view matters less than you think. Book direct on hotelmonterey.co.jp or on Rakuten Travel and take the free-cancellation rate, because February is five months out and nothing is locked. Two things to confirm while you have them: that the room is on a high floor, and that the front desk handles Yamato takkyubin, which you need on the Thursday morning. Fallback if it is full or the price jumps: Toyoko Inn Umeda Nakatsu, which is A$80 a night cheaper and a much smaller room.

checklist.text: Book the flight home
checklist.notes: Done: QF80 + QF1256, Tue 16 Feb, paid Economy Sale fare, one booking. Add the booking reference to the Private vault, not here.

checklist.text: Book the Brisbane → Sydney feeder
checklist.notes: Done: JQ815, 8 Feb, 09:45-12:20, Classic Reward.

checklist.text: Open Manage Booking for QF80 and try to add Economy Plus (extra legroom) with cash or points; pick seats on both flights
checklist.notes: Sale fares cannot be upgraded to Business with points, but the Economy Plus seat product is separate. If it is not offered on this fare, that is that.

checklist.text: Melbourne: 1h35 connection. SmartGate, bag, customs, domestic transfer desk, T1. Skip duty free.
Check the JQ815 booking shows a 20 kg checked bag (reward bookings include one, but the confirmation sometimes shows 0 kg); add a bag if not
Check in online for QF481 the day before (24 h out) so Sydney is bag-drop only
Book Brisbane AIRPARK online for 8-17 Feb
Buy USJ 1-Day Studio Pass + Express Pass 4 with Super Nintendo World entry for Wed 10 Feb (dates open 60 days ahead, so ~12 Dec 2026)
checklist.notes: Official USJ site or Klook (official partner; Klook lets you move the date within 90 days in the same price tier). Buy the day it opens. Create the USJ app account now: since Jan 2026 the app is mandatory for timed-entry tickets.

checklist.text: Travel insurance with the snow-sports add-on (and off-piste cover if you plan to ski Nozawa’s tree runs)
checklist.notes: Standard Australian policies exclude skiing. About A$80 for a week before the add-on. Buy it when you book the first non-refundable thing so cancellation cover starts. Medicare does not cover Japan.

checklist.text: Plan A: reserve the Shinkansen and Shinano seats (smart-EX for Tokyo↔Osaka, JR East site for the Hokuriku)
checklist.notes: Opens 1 month before each travel date: 9 Jan for the 9 Feb trains, 11 Jan for the 11 Feb trains, 16 Jan for the 16 Feb trains. Holiday Thursday trains fill.

checklist.text: Register on Visit Japan Web (immigration + customs QR)
checklist.notes: Australians get 90 days visa-free. Passport just needs to be valid for the stay, but check the expiry anyway.

checklist.text: Install eSIM (Ubigi ~US$14 for 10 GB/7 days, or Airalo) and set up Welcome Suica Mobile (iPhone) or plan to buy a physical Welcome Suica at Narita (Android)
checklist.notes: Suica works in Osaka (ICOCA area) and Nagano too. Google Wallet on non-Japanese Android phones generally cannot hold Suica; the physical Welcome Suica is cash top-up only and expires after 28 days, which is fine for this trip. Top up with Mastercard/Amex in Apple Wallet; some Visa cards fail.

checklist.text: Re-check Melbourne T2 lounge hours for Monday nights (Business Lounge and, if your passes qualify, First Lounge)
Get ¥30,000-50,000 cash (or plan to withdraw at 7-Eleven ATMs on arrival)
checklist.notes: Small restaurants, the standing bars and the buses are still cash-heavy. Both night-out stays are now prepaid, so the only large cash item left is Koyasan at ¥17,600, and only if they have not charged the card by 12 Jan. 7-Eleven ATMs take Australian cards.

checklist.text: Book ski rental online (village shop) for Fri 12, Sat 13, Mon 15 and Tue 16 morning with your boot size in cm; include ski wear if travelling light
checklist.notes: Big boot sizes run out in peak weeks. Pick a shop that opens by 7:45 so Friday is not lost.

checklist.text: Ski: thermals, mid-layer, gloves, goggles, beanie, buff, ski socks x3 (rent jacket/pants/skis/boots/helmet)
Cold: thermals, proper insulated coat, waterproof boots with grip, gloves, beanie, wool socks
checklist.notes: You are leaving a Queensland summer. Hirayu can stay below freezing all day and snows from December to March; Shirakawa-go sits under two metres of it and Koyasan is a cold mountain. The rooms at Hirayu have no air conditioning. Bring more than you think, and remember the small towel for the baths.

checklist.text: Onsen kit: small towel, plus a sense of humour about being naked with strangers
Carry-on for the plane: passport, printed e-ticket, USJ tickets, chargers, Type-A power adapter (Japan is 100 V, US-style plugs), snacks
USJ: through the gate, open the app, claim Super Nintendo World timed entry within seconds (or use the Express Pass slot)
Keep the N’EX round-trip ticket somewhere safe for the trip back to Narita

Tax-free shopping is now a refund at the airport (from Nov 2026): pay the 10% tax at the till, keep receipts and passport scans, and allow time at Narita to claim it back on Nintendo World or Osaka souvenirs
Open the Qantas app → Complimentary Lounge Invitations and confirm the Titanium First Lounge invitations show with an expiry after 8 Feb 2027
checklist.notes: They renew each card anniversary. If the current pair expires before February, the next pair will be issued on the anniversary; check which.

checklist.text: Ask the Nozawa lodging (when booking) whether they accept a courier parcel before arrival, and get their address in Japanese for the takkyubin slip
Reserve the Shinano seats Nagoya → Kiso-Fukushima and Shiojiri → Nagano for Thu 11 Feb, plus the local train times to and from Narai
checklist.notes: Holiday Thursday: reserved seats go. The local Chuo line runs roughly hourly, so match the connections when you book.

checklist.text: Buy simple strap-on crampons (or plan to buy at Workman/Don Quijote in Osaka) for the Togakushi snow walk
Travel insurance for 8-17 Feb (no snow-sports add-on needed for Plan B)
checklist.notes: You now have roughly A$1,190 of prepaid, non-refundable accommodation, so cancellation cover is the point rather than medical alone. Check it covers trip disruption from snow and flight delays. About A$90 for ten days.

checklist.text: Buy simple strap-on crampons, or plan to buy them at Workman or Don Quijote in Osaka
checklist.notes: For the icy lanes at Shirakawa-go, the Okunoin path at Koyasan and the walk between the baths at Hirayu. About ¥1,500 and they fold into a pocket.

checklist.text: Saturday night: check Sunday’s weather. Powder dump = ski; anything else = Togakushi. Check the Alpico winter bus 70 timetable for the first bus and the last bus back
Return rental gear; settle the lodging bill in cash if they do not take cards
Narita T2 check-in closes 18:20 for QF80 (check in online the day before)
Plan B: Koyasan temple night booked (Shojoshin-in, 11 Feb, ¥17,600, cash on arrival)
checklist.notes: Reservation number and QR code in the Private vault.

checklist.text: 12 Jan: check whether the temple charged the registered card; if not, add ¥17,600 to the cash to withdraw at Narita
Plan B: Ootaya gassho farmhouse booked for 13 Feb (¥25,300, 2 meals, prepaid)
checklist.notes: Chosen over Shirakawa-go no Yu and Yui no Sho: the only actual thatched farmhouse of the three, the cheapest, and you already have an onsen night at Hirayu the following evening. Reservation number in the Private vault.

checklist.text: Plan B: Takayama booked as two separate nights (Temple Hotel Takayama Zenkoji, 12-13 and 15-16 Feb, both prepaid)
checklist.notes: Was one four-night booking at A$655.58 covering two nights you sleep elsewhere. The hotel waived the cancellation fee and it was rebooked as A$169.31 (Moon room, 12-13 Feb) plus A$157.21 (Sakura room, 15-16 Feb): A$326.52, saving A$329.06. Both reservation numbers go in the Private vault.

checklist.text: Plan B: email Temple Hotel Takayama Zenkoji about the courier parcel, luggage storage and splitting the booking
checklist.notes: Answered yes to all three: they will receive and hold the Yamato parcel (put the reservation name on the delivery slip), they will store the suitcase on 13 and 14 Feb, and they waived the cancellation fee so the four nights could be rebooked as two.

checklist.text: Plan B: two free-cancellation deadlines for Takayama, 28 Jan (12-13 Feb) and 31 Jan (15-16 Feb)
checklist.notes: Both are 23:59 local. Nothing to do if the trip is going ahead; this is here so a late change does not cost you the rooms by accident.

checklist.text: Plan B: Hirayu no Mori booked for 14 Feb (half board, single, ¥14,550, prepaid)
checklist.notes: Booked and prepaid through Time Design; reservation number is in the Private vault. Loose ends: check the confirmation email from the property actually arrived, and read the cancellation terms so you know where you stand. Tattoos are not a blocker either way, because the private baths are free for guests from 15:00 and nobody else is in them.

checklist.text: Plan B: reserve a counter seat at Gyu-suke (Takayama) for dinner on Mon 15 Feb, about 18:30
checklist.notes: Tabelog or SavorJapan take online bookings 1-2 weeks out; or ask the hotel to call on check-in day. Ajikura Tengoku (walk-in tickets) is the fallback.

checklist.text: Plan B: reserve the Nohi buses Takayama ↔ Shirakawa-go (13 and 14 Feb, late-morning services)
checklist.notes: Opens about a month ahead on nouhibus.co.jp.

checklist.text: Plan B: reserve the Nozomi Tokyo → Shin-Osaka, 9 Feb 11:30, on smart-EX
checklist.notes: Opens 9 Jan at 10:00 Japan time, which is 11:00 at home. smart-EX takes an Australian card, needs no membership fee, and lets you change the train free of charge any number of times before departure. So book it now and move it if QF49 lands late; you are not locked in. This is the only train that is the same in both plans.

checklist.text: Plan B: reserve the Nankai Limited Express Koya, Namba → Koyasan, 11 Feb 10:00
checklist.notes: Opens exactly one month ahead. Nankai is a private railway, so this is booked on Nankai's own site rather than anything JR. Do this one on the day it opens rather than saving it up with the JR bookings: 11 Feb is National Foundation Day, a public holiday, so this train will be busier than a normal Thursday. Reserve rather than turning up. Alternatively buy the Koyasan World Heritage Ticket at Nankai Namba, which includes a discounted seat reservation.

checklist.text: Plan B: reserve the 12 Feb pair, Nozomi Shin-Osaka → Nagoya 12:10 and Limited Express Hida Nagoya → Takayama 13:45
checklist.notes: Both open 12 Jan. The Nozomi is smart-EX. The Hida is NOT: smart-EX only sells Shinkansen, and the Hida is a limited express on a conventional line. Book it through JR West's online reservation (westjr.co.jp, English, takes an overseas card, collect from a machine with the QR), through a reseller like NAVITIME, or simply at a JR ticket machine when you land. The Hida rarely sells out on a Friday, but the 35-minute connection at Nagoya is tight enough that a booked seat is worth having.

checklist.text: Plan B: reserve the 16 Feb trains home: Hida 09:40 Takayama → Nagoya, Nozomi 13:15 Nagoya → Tokyo
checklist.notes: THE ONE DAY EVERYTHING IS OPEN. Japanese reservations open exactly one month before each departure at 10:00 Japan time, so 16 January is the first morning on which every train of the trip is bookable, and nothing on the list has sold out by then. Sit down once and do the lot. Two catches. First, it is three systems, not one checkout: smart-EX for the Nozomi legs, JR West online (or a reseller, or a machine on arrival) for the two Hida legs, and Nankai's own site for Koyasan. Second, the Nankai on the 11th is a public holiday and should not wait until the 16th; do that one on 11 Jan. Of everything here the 09:40 Hida matters most, because it runs about hourly and it is the train connecting to an international flight, so book it the morning it opens.

questions.question: Plan A (ski) or Plan B (no skiing)?
questions.why: Both use the flights already booked and the same Osaka and USJ days; they split on Thursday 11 Feb. Plan A: Nozawa Onsen for five nights, three ski days plus a rural Sunday, hinges on finding a solo room in a sold-out week. Plan B: Takayama as the base for four days, with two nights out in great places (a temple at Koyasan, a farmhouse at Shirakawa-go), free afternoons and a free day, and no start before 9:30 except USJ, which the Express Pass makes optional. No dependence on Nozawa, and about A$500 cheaper because there are no lifts or rental. Lost workdays are identical. The plan switch at the top of the menu flips every page between them.
options: Plan A: ski trip (Nozawa Onsen)
Plan B: Takayama base with Koyasan and Shirakawa-go nights out
Hybrid: Plan B with two of the Takayama nights swapped for Nozawa without skiing (onsen village, snow, food)
questions.recommendation: Decide by accommodation: if a Nozawa room lands by late October, Plan A. If not, Plan B is not a consolation prize; the Koyasan and Shirakawa-go nights are two of the best things you can do in Japan in winter, and every bed in it is easier to get.

questions.question: Kamakura or Yamaguchi: can either fit?
questions.why: Kamakura (Great Buddha, Hase-dera, the Enoden tram along the coast) is an hour from Tokyo and a proper day. On this trip Tokyo is only a transit point: the morning you land (jet-lagged, heading to Osaka) and the afternoon you fly home (Takayama to Narita already takes the day). Fitting it means leaving Takayama a day early, forfeiting the prepaid Monday night in Takayama, paying for a Tokyo hotel and moving the suitcase again, for about three hours in Kamakura with the airport clock running. Yamaguchi (Rurikoji pagoda, Akiyoshido cave, Motonosumi shrine, Hagi) is at the far western end of Honshu, two and a half hours beyond Osaka by Shinkansen and spread out enough to need a car; it is a two- or three-day region of its own, not a detour.
options: Leave both for another trip (planned)
Kamakura on 16 Feb: leave Takayama on the 15th, sleep in Tokyo, 3 h in Kamakura before Narita
Yamaguchi: not possible without dropping Koyasan or the Takayama days
questions.recommendation: Leave both. Kamakura is the first thing to do on a future Tokyo-based trip (spring or autumn, weekday). Yamaguchi pairs with Hiroshima and Miyajima on a western trip.
questions.answer: Neither this trip. Kamakura first on the next Tokyo trip; Yamaguchi with Hiroshima on a western trip.

questions.question: Ski base: Nozawa Onsen, Myoko (Akakura Onsen) or Hakuba?
questions.why: You said “south island”, which does not exist for skiing (Japan’s ski areas are on Hokkaido in the north and in the Nagano/Niigata mountains on the main island). Given Narita arrival + Osaka + a week, Nagano/Niigata is the only sensible region. Nozawa is the closest thing to Banff: a real village, walkable, hot springs, mountain rising straight off it, local food. It is also the most Australian of the villages and the busiest over the 11-14 Feb long weekend.
options: Nozawa Onsen (planned): Banff-like village, big mountain, local food, busiest and priciest of the three that weekend
Myoko / Akakura Onsen: quieter, cheaper, more Japanese, 13-16 m of snow, smaller mountain, fiddlier buses
Hakuba: biggest terrain and most Banff-like scale, but a sprawl of villages linked by buses and very international
questions.recommendation: Nozawa Onsen. If you decide “not hyped” matters more than terrain, switch to Myoko: the plan only changes at the Nagano end (Shinkansen to Joetsu-Myoko instead of Iiyama).

questions.question: Trip shape: Universal Studios first (Wednesday) or ski first and fly home from Osaka?
questions.why: Wed 10 Feb is the only calm weekday for USJ in the window (Thu 11 is a public holiday and the weekend follows, plus the tail of Lunar New Year travel). That forces the skiing onto the long weekend. The alternative is ski Wed-Fri (quieter slopes on Wed), then USJ on Mon 15 and fly Jetstar Osaka → Brisbane at 9:45pm that night, no Tokyo backtrack.
options: USJ Wed 10, ski Fri-Mon, fly QF62 Narita → Brisbane Mon 15 (planned)
Ski Wed-Fri, Osaka Sat-Mon, USJ Mon 15, Jetstar JQ24 Osaka → Brisbane Mon 15 night
questions.recommendation: Keep USJ on the Wednesday. Super Nintendo World on a crowded day is the thing most likely to spoil the trip, and Nozawa is big enough to absorb a weekend if you start at 8:30. Monday morning skiing is the bonus.

questions.question: Give up Sunday’s skiing for Togakushi and Zenko-ji, or fly home Tuesday to keep three full ski days?
questions.why: You asked for a rural day and said a ski day could go. Narai-juku is now built into Thursday’s travel day at no cost. Sunday is the worst ski day (long-weekend crowds), so it is the cheapest one to trade for Togakushi’s cedar avenue and Zenko-ji. That leaves Friday, Saturday and Monday morning on skis. Flying home Tuesday 16 instead would add a full quiet Monday on the slopes for about A$150 of lodging plus a day of leave.

questions.recommendation: As planned, with the powder-day escape hatch: if Sunday dawns dumping, ski and skip Togakushi.
questions.answer: Tue 16 is booked, so Monday is a full ski day and Sunday is the rural day, with the powder-day swap written into Sunday’s notes.

questions.question: Which rural stop, if you want a different one?

Shirakawa-go’s farmhouses are the postcard but are 4+ hours each way from Nozawa and heavily touristed; not worth it on this trip. Matsumoto castle is a city.
options: Togakushi + Zenko-ji (planned): mountain shrine, cedars, soba, snow walk
Obuse + Zenko-ji: gentler, indoor-heavy, good if the weather is foul
Nothing beyond Narai
questions.recommendation: Togakushi, with Obuse as the bad-weather substitute.
